messages.content:
Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000004

From text 'aydogan2024reviewofin pages 17-19'.

Beytullah Aydogan and Kevin Chou. Review of in situ detection and ex situ characterization of porosity in laser powder bed fusion metal additive manufacturing. Metals, 14:669, Jun 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/met14060669, doi:10.3390/met14060669. This article has 40 citations.

The excerpt only partially addresses the question. It explains that optical or metallographic approaches are destructive and restricted to polished cross-sectional regions, so the examined area may not represent the whole LPBF specimen; a section can appear defect-free while pores remain elsewhere or beneath the surface. This sampling limitation can lead to an underestimate of total porosity. However, the provided passage does not explicitly describe the mechanical pore-smearing mechanism caused by metallographic polishing, nor does it give a quantitative comparison between optical-microscopy porosity measurements and X-ray CT measurements. It does state that X-ray CT is used for three-dimensional pore location and size determination because of its high accuracy, whereas optical/SEM examination provides detailed characterization but is confined to cross-sectional analysis. For Archimedes measurements, the excerpt reports that density estimates differed from X-ray results by approximately up to 3%. Archimedes is nondestructive, simple, and inexpensive, but it reports only overall density—the combined effect of concealed voids—and cannot identify pore type or shape. Thus, optical microscopy may underestimate bulk porosity relative to volumetric X-ray CT, while Archimedes provides an overall density-based estimate that was within about 3% of X-ray density in the cited comparison.


---

## pqac-00000005

From text 'cerezo2024tomographyoflaser pages 7-9'.

Pablo M. Cerezo, Jose A. Aguilera, Antonio Garcia-Gonzalez, and Pablo Lopez-Crespo. Tomography of laser powder bed fusion maraging steel. Materials, 17:891, Feb 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17040891, doi:10.3390/ma17040891. This article has 8 citations.

The excerpt does not explicitly describe metallographic polishing or pore smearing. It does, however, identify the methodological limitation behind optical microscopy (OM): OM characterizes pores on a polished two-dimensional surface, whereas X-ray computed tomography (CT) evaluates the full three-dimensional pore volume. A 2D section can cut through a pore in a way that makes it appear more circular and uniform, while the unmeasured third dimension hides pore non-uniformity. Consequently, 3D CT provides a broader and more precise assessment of pore dimensions and shape, including more reliable maximum and minimum pore sizes. In the 18Ni300 LPBF sample, CT measured relative porosity below 0.1% throughout the construction axis, corresponding to relative density above 99.9%, including surface porosity. OM measurements reported porosity as high as 0.185% of the examined section, indicating that the optical result was higher than the CT result in this study. The excerpt does not provide Archimedes density measurements or a direct numerical comparison with Archimedes results. It also does not explicitly attribute the OM–CT difference to polishing-induced smearing; that mechanism would need support from another section or source.


---

## pqac-00000006

Abstract:
This study explores the effect of heat treatment on the microstructural characteristics and corrosion resistance of 316L stainless steels (SSs) produced via laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), focusing on anisotropic corrosion behavior—a relatively less explored phenomenon in LPBF 316L SSs. By systematically analyzing the effects of varying heat treatment temperatures (500 °C, 750 °C, and 1000 °C), this work uncovers critical correlations between microstructural evolution and corrosion properties. The findings include the identification of anisotropic corrosion resistance between horizontal (XY) and vertical (XZ) planes, with the vertical plane demonstrating higher pitting and repassivation potentials but greater post-repassivation current densities. Furthermore, this study highlights reductions in grain size, dislocation density, and melt pool boundaries with increasing heat treatment temperatures, which collectively diminishes corrosion resistance. These insights advance the understanding of processing–structure–property relationships in additively manufactured metals, providing practical guidelines for optimizing thermal post-processing to enhance material performance in corrosive environments.

Abstract:
This article overviews the scientific results of the microstructural features observed in 316 L stainless steel manufactured by the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) method obtained by the authors, and discusses the results with respect to the recently published literature. Microscopic features of the LPBF microstructure, i.e., epitaxial nucleation, cellular structure, microsegregation, porosity, competitive colony growth, and solidification texture, were experimentally studied by scanning and transmission electron microscopy, diffraction methods, and atom probe tomography. The influence of laser power and laser scanning speed on the microstructure was discussed in the perspective of governing the microstructure by controlling the process parameters. It was shown that the three-dimensional (3D) zig-zag solidification texture observed in the LPBF 316 L was related to the laser scanning strategy. The thermal stability of the microstructure was investigated under isothermal annealing conditions. It was shown that the cells formed at solidification started to disappear at about 800 °C, and that this process leads to a substantial decrease in hardness. Colony boundaries, nevertheless, were quite stable, and no significant grain growth was observed after heat treatment at 1050 °C. The observed experimental results are discussed with respect to the fundamental knowledge of the solidification processes, and compared with the existing literature data.

Abstract:
Molten pool geometry, whose surface parameters may be extrapolated through direct process observations, has been identified as a fundamental indicator of stability in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). However, a parameter that cannot be directly measured on industrial systems by means of conventional sensing equipment is the molten pool depth. Indeed, methods based on x-ray imaging demonstrated in the literature have helped to better understand the process. However, retrofitting such solutions to industrial systems does not appear as a viable route currently. Within the present investigation, a nonintrusive sensing method for the indirect measurement of subsurface molten pool geometry based on the detection of surface oscillations is presented. The analysis of frames acquired using a high-speed camera and a secondary illumination light allows the identification of the crests of capillary waves through bright reflections on the surface of the molten pool. The characteristic oscillation frequency of the surface ripples may be correlated with the penetration depth or to other subsurface geometrical parameters. Proof of concept testing of the sensing principle was conducted on two different materials, namely, AISI316L and IN718, by means of single track LPBF depositions. Experiments were conducted at different levels of laser emission power to induce variations in molten pool characteristics. The process was observed by employing an off-axis illumination light and a high-speed camera, which allowed acquisitions with high spatial and temporal resolution. The acquired frames were postprocessed to extract the oscillation indicator, and analysis of the power spectral density of the signal allowed for the identification of the oscillation frequency. Results show that oscillation frequencies range from 3 to 5.5 kHz. Molten pool penetration depth and cross-sectional area could be correlated with the oscillation frequencies for the inline detection of these parameters during LPBF depositions. For both materials, higher oscillation frequencies corresponded to a shallower molten pool and a smaller mass of molten material. Moreover, different characteristic curves of oscillation frequency variations as a function of the melt pool cross-sectional area were determined for IN718 and AISI316L.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Residual stress remains a significant challenge in the widespread adoption of the Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) process, due to its detrimental impact on dimensional accuracy and post-processing requirements and hinders further processing with methods such as welding. Different strategies have already been explored to reduce or mitigate these stresses, including preheating, alternating scan strategies, and heat treatments. In this study, a less commonly investigated approach is examined: the influence of melt pool geometry—specifically layer height and track width—on the residual stresses in LPBF-manufactured 316L stainless steel. By systematically varying these parameters, the resulting internal stress states are compared by distortion measurements of cantilever parts to determine potential correlations and mechanisms of influence. The findings aim to contribute to a deeper understanding of process–structure–property relationships in LPBF and to offer a new avenue for stress control through geometrical process parameter optimization. It can be concluded that among all the strategies for preventing and mitigating residual stress in LPBF, the examined approach has a relatively small influence. The results show that increasing layer thickness and decreasing spot diameter have beneficial effects on the resulting deformations.</jats:p>

Microstructural characterization of Fe-9\%Cr ODS steel produced via selective laser melting This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt provides one explicit electrolytic etching recipe: 10% oxalic acid in deionized water, applied at 6 V for 20 seconds. It states that the voltage and electrolyte selection came from PSI internal knowledge, while the 20-second duration was established by studying microstructural evolution with increasing etching time. The excerpt also describes chemical etching with V2A reagent and a contrast medium. V2A etching was tested at room temperature and at 50 °C, each for 20 seconds. Room-temperature etching produced a clearly visible structure, whereas the 50 °C treatment caused overt etching, stains or large holes, so the procedure was subsequently limited to room temperature. Cleaning after etching was performed using static acetone, ethanol, and deionized-water baths rather than ultrasonic cleaning, because heating and residual acid/acetone interaction could worsen surface definition. The supplied text does not provide recipes or application times for aqua regia, Kalling’s No. 2, or glyceregia, and it concerns Fe-9%Cr ODS steel rather than LPBF 316L stainless steel. Therefore, only the oxalic-acid and V2A conditions are directly supported by this excerpt.

## 2. Process Induced Preheating in Laser Powder Bed Fusion Monitored by Thermography and Its Influence on the Microstructure of 316L Stainless Steel Parts

    title = "Process Induced Preheating in Laser Powder Bed Fusion Monitored by Thermography and Its Influence on the Microstructure of 316L Stainless Steel Parts",
    year = "2021",
    journal = "Metals",
    volume = "11",
    pages = "1063",
    month = "Jul",
    doi = "10.3390/met11071063",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/met11071063",

Abstract:
Undetected and undesired microstructural variations in components produced by laser powder bed fusion are a major challenge, especially for safety-critical components. In this study, an in-depth analysis of the microstructural features of 316L specimens produced by laser powder bed fusion at different levels of volumetric energy density and different levels of inter layer time is reported. The study has been conducted on specimens with an application relevant build height (>100 mm). Furthermore, the evolution of the intrinsic preheating temperature during the build-up of specimens was monitored using a thermographic in-situ monitoring set-up. By applying recently determined emissivity values of 316L powder layers, real temperatures could be quantified. Heat accumulation led to preheating temperatures of up to about 600 °C. Significant differences in the preheating temperatures were discussed with respect to the individual process parameter combinations, including the build height. A strong effect of the inter layer time on the heat accumulation was observed. A shorter inter layer time resulted in an increase of the preheating temperature by more than a factor of 2 in the upper part of the specimens compared to longer inter layer times. This, in turn, resulted in heterogeneity of the microstructure and differences in material properties within individual specimens. The resulting differences in the microstructure were analyzed using electron back scatter diffraction and scanning electron microscopy. Results from chemical analysis as well as electron back scatter diffraction measurements indicated stable conditions in terms of chemical alloy composition and austenite phase content for the used set of parameter combinations. However, an increase of the average grain size by more than a factor of 2.5 could be revealed within individual specimens. Additionally, differences in feature size of the solidification cellular substructure were examined and a trend of increasing cell sizes was observed. This trend was attributed to differences in solidification rate and thermal gradients induced by differences in scanning velocity and preheating temperature. A change of the thermal history due to intrinsic preheating could be identified as the main cause of this heterogeneity. It was induced by critical combinations of the energy input and differences in heat transfer conditions by variations of the inter layer time. ## pqac-00000026

Simon Schmid, Johannes Krabusch, Thomas Schromm, Shi Jieqing, Stefan Ziegelmeier, Christian Ulrich Grosse, and Johannes Henrich Schleifenbaum. A new approach for automated measuring of the melt pool geometry in laser-powder bed fusion. Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 6:269-279, Mar 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-021-00173-7, doi:10.1007/s40964-021-00173-7. This article has 43 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies the measurable quantities from etched LPBF cross-sections as melt-pool welding depth (dmp) and width (wmp), obtained after segmentation of the melt-pool boundaries. It emphasizes that conventional studies generally measure melt pools manually and often restrict the analysis to single tracks or the top layer, because neighboring tracks and subsequent layers remelt earlier pools. The proposed method instead evaluates melt pools throughout the specimen cross-section, including partly visible remelted pools, thereby enabling many pools to be measured and improving statistical analysis. However, these pages do not specify how many melt pools should be averaged, nor do they provide a numerical counting rule for pools in the last layer. Section orientation is important: when the scan direction is rotated by an angle such as 67° between layers, an inclined section plane makes melt pools appear distorted and creates patterns that are more difficult to analyze. The study therefore uses a 90° scan-direction rotation for its melt-pool measurements. The excerpt does not quantify the resulting dimensional error or give a correction formula for section-angle distortion.

## pqac-00000027

From text 'soares2026processoptimizationofa pages 81-86'.

MA Soares. Process optimization of metal 3d printing through thermographic analysis of the melt pool. Unknown journal, 2026.

The excerpt describes measuring melt-pool width and depth on etched/metallographic cross-sections using a Keyence VHX-7000 optical microscope and its image-analysis software, at 500× and 1000× magnification. For each single track, width and depth were measured from transverse cross-sectional views and averaged over eight measurements. The top view was instead used to characterize the full track and correlate in-process thermal observations with post-process metallography. Reported uncertainty was approximately ±5–40 μm, combining track-to-track variability with the operator-dependent identification of melt-pool boundaries. The excerpt does not specify how many distinct melt pools should be counted in the final layer, nor does it give a protocol for selecting pools in that layer. It also does not discuss the effect of cutting or sectioning angle relative to the laser scan direction, such as apparent elongation or distortion of melt-pool width and depth. Therefore, the only directly supported averaging instruction is eight cross-sectional measurements per single track; procedures for last-layer pool selection and angular correction must be obtained from another source or methodological context.

The excerpt describes measuring melt-pool width and depth from etched transverse cross-sections using a Keyence VHX 7000 optical microscope and its image-analysis software. For each single track, the reported width and depth were obtained by averaging eight measurements taken from cross-sectional views. The text does not specify how many distinct melt pools should be counted in the final printed layer, nor does it provide a rule for selecting pools in the last layer. It also does not discuss the geometric effect of cutting the section at an angle relative to the laser scan direction, such as the apparent elongation or broadening of melt-pool dimensions caused by an oblique section. Therefore, the excerpt supports an eight-measurement averaging procedure but cannot establish a last-layer counting protocol or an angle-correction method. Measurement uncertainty was reported as approximately ±5–40 μm, attributed to both track-to-track process variability and the operator-dependent difficulty of identifying melt-pool boundaries. The excerpt also distinguishes top-view characterization of the complete track from transverse cross-sectional measurements of width and depth.

From text 'soares2026processoptimizationofa pages 74-81'.

MA Soares. Process optimization of metal 3d printing through thermographic analysis of the melt pool. Unknown journal, 2026.

The excerpt provides only partial guidance for measuring melt-pool dimensions from post-process cross-sections. messages.content:
Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000042

From text 'zheng2021defectanalysisof pages 10-14'.

Zhi-Ping Zheng, L. Peng, and Di Wang. Defect analysis of 316 l stainless steel prepared by lpbf additive manufacturing processes. Coatings, 11:1562, Dec 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/coatings11121562, doi:10.3390/coatings11121562. This article has 34 citations.

The excerpt indicates that chemical etching can substantially modify the apparent morphology surrounding LPBF pores and defects, making pre-etch imaging important for reliable porosity characterization. In low-energy material, pores and lack-of-fusion defects are associated with unfused powder, incomplete molten-metal filling, and non-filled gaps. At the optimal energy density, defects were small and spherical, whereas excessive energy input caused over-melting, very large grains, reduced corrosion resistance, and corrosion trenches in the melt pools. These trenches and grooves are produced by the corrosion/etching process rather than necessarily representing original pores, and they can obscure, enlarge, split, or visually resemble pore boundaries. Consequently, porosity measurements made only after etching may confuse etch-induced grooves or preferentially corroded regions with true voids and may alter estimates of pore size, shape, number, and area fraction. The excerpt also contrasts conditions where pores were clearly visible with etched microstructures in which pores were “almost invisible,” showing that etching can affect defect visibility in either direction. Imaging the unetched surface first preserves the original pore geometry; etched metallography can then be used separately to study melt-pool structure, lack of fusion, and microstructural development.


---

## pqac-00000043

From text 'cerezo2024tomographyoflaser pages 4-7'.

Pablo M. Cerezo, Jose A. Aguilera, Antonio Garcia-Gonzalez, and Pablo Lopez-Crespo. Tomography of laser powder bed fusion maraging steel. Materials, 17:891, Feb 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17040891, doi:10.3390/ma17040891. This article has 8 citations.

The excerpt supports imaging LPBF porosity by X-ray CT before metallographic preparation because CT records the three-dimensional internal pore network without sectioning or surface preparation. It can identify both elongated keyhole pores and spherical gas-inclusion pores, measure their volumes and surface areas, and calculate three-dimensional shape descriptors such as sphericity and aspect ratio. Metallographic optical microscopy, by contrast, examines only selected polished cross-sections and determines pore size from two-dimensional pixel measurements; therefore, it can miss pores between sections or distort their apparent geometry. The excerpt does not specifically report an etching experiment or quantify how etching changes pore boundaries. It does establish that pore measurements depend on image segmentation, resolution, polishing, and the measurement method. Consequently, any etching that changes, obscures, or visually redefines the material–void interface could alter the apparent pore perimeter and area in optical images, affecting circularity, aspect ratio, and estimated porosity. CT data acquired before etching provide a reference for the original pore morphology and volume. The study also cautions that limited resolution produces greater error for very small pore volumes, while the error decreases as pore volume increases.


---

## pqac-00000044

From text 'cerezo2024tomographyoflaser pages 7-9'.

Pablo M. Cerezo, Jose A. Aguilera, Antonio Garcia-Gonzalez, and Pablo Lopez-Crespo. Tomography of laser powder bed fusion maraging steel. Materials, 17:891, Feb 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17040891, doi:10.3390/ma17040891. This article has 8 citations.

The excerpt does not directly discuss etching or require imaging before etching. It does show why the initial, unetched metallographic image is important for reliable comparison: optical microscopy (OM) provides a 2D measurement of pore area and shape, whereas X-ray CT provides 3D pore volume and morphology. A 2D section can make a pore appear more circular depending on the plane intersected, and therefore may overestimate circularity or aspect ratio and fail to represent the pore’s non-uniform three-dimensional boundary. The authors report that 3D analysis gives a broader and more accurate distribution of pore dimensions, while 2D measurements can produce different apparent morphology and porosity values. Consequently, any preparation step that changes contrast or the apparent pore boundary—including etching—could alter segmentation, measured pore area, circularity, and calculated porosity. Imaging before etching preserves the original polished-section boundary and provides a baseline; post-etch images should be interpreted cautiously because etching may reveal, obscure, or visually modify pore edges and nearby material. The excerpt supports the general measurement concern but does not specify the direction or magnitude of etching-induced changes.

Abstract:
High-energy diffraction microscopy (HEDM) in-situ mechanical testing experiments offer unique insight into the evolving deformation state within polycrystalline materials. These experiments rely on a sophisticated analysis of the diffraction data to instantiate a 3D reconstruction of grains and other microstructural features associated with the test volume. For microstructures of engineering alloys that are highly twinned and contain numerous features around the estimated spatial resolution of HEDM reconstructions, the accuracy of the reconstructed microstructure is not known. In this study, we address this uncertainty by characterizing the same HEDM sample volume using destructive serial sectioning (SS) that has higher spatial resolution. The SS experiment was performed on an Inconel 625 alloy sample that had undergone HEDM in-situ mechanical testing to a small amount of plastic strain (~ 0.7%), which was part of the Air Force Research Laboratory Additive Manufacturing (AM) Modeling Series. A custom-built automated multi-modal SS system was used to characterize the entire test volume, with a spatial resolution of approximately 1 µm. Epi-illumination optical microscopy images, backscattered electron images, and electron backscattered diffraction maps were collected on every section. All three data modes were utilized and custom data fusion protocols were developed for 3D reconstruction of the test volume. The grain data were homogenized and downsampled to 2 µm as input for Challenge 4 of the AM Modeling Series, which is available at the Materials Data Facility repository.

Abstract:
Sedimentary rocks contain a unique record of the evolution of the Earth system. Deciphering this record requires a robust understanding of the identity, origin, composition, and post-depositional history of individual constituents. Petrographic analysis informed by Scanning Electron Microscope - Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) mineral mapping can reveal the mineral identity, morphology and petrological context of each imaged grain, making it a valuable tool in the Earth Scientist’s analytical arsenal. Recent technological developments, including quantitative deconvolution of mixed-phase spectra (producing “mixels”), now allow rapid quantitative SEM-EDS-based analysis of a broad range of sedimentary rocks, including the previously troublesome fine-grained lithologies that comprise most of the sedimentary record. Here, we test the reliability and preferred mineral mapping work flow of a modern Field-Emission scanning electron microscope equipped with the Thermofisher Scientific Maps Mineralogy mineral mapping system, focusing on mud/siltstones and calcareous shales. We demonstrate that SEM-EDS mineral mapping that implements 1) a strict error minimization spectral matching approach and 2) spectral deconvolution to produce ‘mixels’ for mixed-phase X-ray volumes can robustly identify individual grains and produce quantitative mineralogical data sets comparable to conventional X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis (R 2 > 0.95). The correlation between SEM-EDS and XRD-derived mineralogy is influenced by mineral abundance, processing modes and mapped area characteristics. Minerals with higher abundance (>10 wt%) show better correlation, likely the result of increased uncertainty for XRD quantification of low-abundance phases. Automated spectral deconvolution to produce ‘mixels’ greatly reduces the proportion of unclassified pixels, especially in the fine-grained fraction, ultimately improving mineral identification and quantification. Mapping of larger areas benefits bulk mineralogy analysis, while customized area size and shape allows high-resolution in situ mineralogical analysis. Finally, we review SEM-EDS-based mineral mapping applications in the Earth Sciences, via case studies illustrating 1) approaches for the quantitative differentiation of various mineral components including detrital (allogenic), syndepositional (authigenic) and burial diagenetic phases, 2) the origin and significance of lamination, 3) the effectiveness and appropriateness of sequential leaching in geochemical studies, and 4) the utility of mineral maps to identify target grains within specific petrological contexts for in situ geochemical or geochronological analysis.

Abstract:

 Modified feedstock containing 316L stainless steel powder along with 1 wt.% of different nitrides, namely aluminum nitride (AlN), boron nitride (BN), titanium nitride (TiN), iron nitride (FexN) and silicon nitride (Si3N4) were laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) printed. The influence of these nitrides on the surface roughness, microhardness, and wear resistance of LPBF-316L has been investigated. The BN addition has significantly improved the microhardness and wear resistance of LPBF-316L, whereas the surface roughness has declined. The improved properties in LPBF-316L with BN addition were correlated with the altered microstructure.

{"answer": "## Best Practice for Preparing and Imaging Cross-Sections of LPBF 316L Thin Walls: Porosity and Melt-Pool Depth Measurement by SEM

### 1. Cutting, Mounting, Grinding, and Polishing

**Cutting.** Cross-sections should be produced using precision diamond saws with water cooling or lubrication to minimize heat damage and surface deformation (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000002). Abrasive cut-off wheels, while faster, produce a wider kerf and more subsurface deformation; if used, they must be selected specifically for austenitic stainless steels and followed by sufficient grinding to remove the heat-affected zone (pqac-00000023). Wire-cutting (EDM) has also been used to extract sections more than 5 mm from build surfaces, with section thicknesses of approximately 2 mm (pqac-00000000). For the described thin-wall geometry (1.27 mm thick), precision diamond sawing is preferred because it produces a narrow kerf (~0.3–0.5 mm) with minimal subsurface deformation, which is critical when grinding must stop at a defined centreline plane. Protecting surfaces from clamping damage with rubber or metal shims is recommended (pqac-00000023).

**Conductive hot mounting and edge retention.** For SEM imaging, conductive mounts are essential. Westin et al. report positive experience with phenolic resin (PhenoCure™) and epoxy-based (EpoMet® G) mounting compounds (pqac-00000023). Cold-mount epoxies provide lower shrinkage and better edge retention for microstructure analysis but require several hours to cure and are softer, which may reduce polishing efficiency (pqac-00000023). For the top edge of a thin wall where melt-pool depth is measured in the last layer, edge retention is critical; conductive epoxy mounting or use of a nickel-plating or copper-plating technique before mounting can protect the edge from rounding during grinding and polishing. Chamfering or rounding of mount edges before grinding extends SiC paper and polishing cloth life (pqac-00000024).

**Grinding and polishing sequence.** The recommended automated preparation sequence, adapted from Westin et al. (doi:10.1007/s40194-025-02286-x, Tables 3–4) for 25 mm diameter embedded stainless steel specimens on a Struers Tegramin 30, is as follows:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

This protocol was developed for DED-arc stainless steel welds and AM deposits and has proven suitable for austenitic stainless steels with varying microstructures (pqac-00000024). Ronneberg et al. used a similar approach for LPBF 316L (200 W, 750 mm/s, 110 µm hatch, 50 µm layer, chessboard strategy on a Concept Laser): SiC grinding papers, diamond suspensions down to 1 µm, and final polishing with 0.06 µm (60 nm) colloidal silica suspension, followed by electrolytic etching (pqac-00000031). Vallejo et al. used SiC grinding papers and diamond paste polishing with a 0.05 µm colloidal silica final finish on LPBF 316L built on an SLM 125HL (200 W, 800 mm/s, 0.12 mm hatch, 0.03 mm layer) (pqac-00000034).

**Controlling material removal depth.** When grinding to a centreline plane, one approach is to mark the target plane with a permanent pen on the outer surface and account for expected grinding consumption (pqac-00000023). Inspection every 30 seconds during hand grinding—checking that the surface is flat, fully exposed, and free of misaligned scratches—is recommended (pqac-00000024). For automated preparation, the planar grinding step (SiC 500 or grinding stone) is repeated until all samples in the holder are planar before proceeding.

### 2. How Polishing Changes Measured Porosity

**Smearing.** Mechanical grinding and polishing can plastically deform metal over pore openings, partially or fully closing small voids and causing the measured porosity to underestimate the true value. This effect is widely recognized (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000045). Bahshwan (doi:10.3390/ma19214527) noted that "artifacts such as smeared pores can arise due to polishing" in LPBF 316L, though the magnitude was not quantified (pqac-00000045). Xavier et al. (doi:10.1007/s00170-019-04597-y) similarly noted that grinding and polishing "may affect the sizes and shapes of pores due to metal smearing" (pqac-00000030). Colloidal silica (OP-S) has a mild chemical–mechanical attack that helps remove the deformed layer, but over-polishing can create relief at phase boundaries and alter contrast (pqac-00000025).

**Comparison with X-ray CT and Archimedes.** Methods do not always agree, and the direction of discrepancy is not universal. In one LPBF 316L comparison by Zheng et al. (doi:10.3390/coatings11121562), optical metallography measured approximately 3.70% porosity, Archimedes gave 3.88%, and XCT yielded 3.00% for the same high-porosity sample, with the difference partly attributed to XCT's inability to resolve defects smaller than ~5 µm (pqac-00000009). In a low-porosity LPBF 316L study by Yusuf et al. (doi:10.3390/met7020064), Archimedes measured ~0.82% average porosity while XCT measured ~0.61% (pqac-00000010). Tajalli et al. (doi:10.1007/s13632-026-01349-9) compared OM, Archimedes, and XCT for 316L-2.5Cu and found close agreement for dense samples but divergence for samples with localized defect concentrations (pqac-00000008). XCT is generally considered more representative for three-dimensional pore characterization but has resolution limits; Archimedes provides only bulk density without pore-level information and is sensitive to surface defects (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006). **Strongly supported conclusion:** no single method is unbiased, and cross-validation is essential (pqac-00000007).

**Checking for artifacts.** Repeating the final polishing step and re-imaging can reveal whether apparent pore closure changes with additional material removal. Comparison with Archimedes density on the same specimen provides an independent bulk check. When feasible, CT scanning before sectioning provides a ground-truth reference (pqac-00000007).

### 3. Imaging Porosity: Optical vs. SEM BSE/SE, Magnification, Area, and Standards

**Imaging mode.** Ronneberg et al. used a Hirox RH-2000 digital microscope for porosity characterisation at a resolution of 2.61 µm/pixel and separately used a Hitachi S-3400N SEM with backscattered electron (BSE) detection at 13 kV accelerating voltage and ~8 mm working distance for microstructural examination of etched samples (pqac-00000031). BSE imaging on unetched, polished surfaces provides strong atomic-number contrast between the steel matrix and voids (appearing black), making segmentation straightforward. SE imaging also shows pores via topographic contrast but can be confused by polishing scratches. For the Thermo Fisher Apreo C (a field-emission SEM), BSE imaging at 10–15 kV is generally preferred for porosity because it provides flat, composition-sensitive contrast with minimal topographic noise.

**Magnification and pixel size.** Vallejo et al. used 100× optical magnification with five micrographs per section for porosity quantification (pqac-00000034). Ronneberg et al. used 2.61 µm/pixel and stitched mosaics covering at least 1000 mm² per section (pqac-00000031). For SEM, comparable coverage requires lower magnification (≤100×) with automated stage tiling and stitching. The minimum resolved pore size is fundamentally limited by the pixel size: Ronneberg et al. filtered out objects smaller than 25 µm² (< 4 pixels), corresponding to an equivalent circular diameter of ~5.6 µm (pqac-00000031). As a practical minimum, a pore should span at least 3–4 pixels in each direction to be reliably segmented.

**Area required for statistical significance.** Ronneberg et al. imaged >1000 mm² per section orientation for LPBF 316L at ~0.3–0.7% porosity to attain adequate statistics (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032). For the described thin walls (~1.27 × 7.6 mm cross-section = ~9.7 mm² per wall), the analysable core area (≥0.2 mm from faces, ≥1 mm from base and top) is roughly 0.87 × 5.6 mm ≈ 4.9 mm² per wall, so seven walls per mount ≈ 34 mm² of core area. At very low porosity (~0.1%), this small area may contain few pores, increasing statistical uncertainty. ASTM E1245 (doi:10.31399/asm.hb.v09.a0003789) specifies automatic image analysis of inclusions or phases with measurement of area fraction and uncertainty, requiring a sufficient number of fields to reduce the 95% confidence interval to an acceptable fraction of the measured value (pqac-00000047). **Weakly supported estimate:** for 0.1% porosity with ≤20% relative uncertainty, areas of several hundred mm² or more may be needed; at 1–5% porosity, tens of mm² can suffice (extrapolated from Ronneberg's practice of >1000 mm² for ~0.5% porosity).

**Number of sections per specimen.** Ronneberg et al. examined both horizontal and vertical sections for each build orientation to capture anisotropy and used the geometric mean of area-fraction porosity from two orthogonal sections to estimate volumetric relative density (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032). For the thin-wall geometry where a single lengthwise centreline section is taken, one section per wall is the minimum; repeating on a parallel section offset by ~0.3 mm would check for spatial variability.

### 4. Segmentation and Pore Classification

**Thresholding.** Grey-level thresholding is the standard approach. Mohr et al. used a fixed threshold of 136 (on an unspecified grey scale) for all cross-sections, applied via IMS Client software (pqac-00000039). Ronneberg et al. used ImageJ's "Analyse Particles" function (pqac-00000031). The PoreAnalyzer open-source tool (doi:10.3390/app11136086) and the RAPID tool (doi:10.3390/ma19214527) provide automated workflows for batch processing of optical micrographs with threshold tuning and morphological operators (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000045). Otsu's method or manual threshold selection with visual verification are common; the key is consistency across all images.

**Pore classification criteria.** The following table summarizes literature-derived heuristics for distinguishing lack-of-fusion (LoF), keyhole, and gas pores based on 2D (circularity, aspect ratio) and 3D (sphericity) shape descriptors:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

Key sources: Kan et al. (doi:10.1007/s10853-022-06990-7) describe gas pores as generally <100 µm and spherical, LoF pores as large and irregular, and keyhole pores as large and spherical (pqac-00000015). Nudelis and Mayr (doi:10.3390/met11121912) proposed a 3D CT-based classification using sphericity ≥0.6, compactness ≥0.4, and BB-factor ≥0.6 for spherical pores, with diameter classes of ≤100 µm, 100–200 µm, and >200 µm (pqac-00000012). Ellendt et al. (doi:10.3390/app11136086) used circularity ≥95% for gas pores and aspect ratio >5 for cracks in 2D optical analysis (pqac-00000016). These are heuristics rather than universal boundaries and should be validated for the specific process window.

### 5. Etching to Reveal Melt-Pool Boundaries

**Why porosity must be imaged before etching.** Chemical or electrolytic etching preferentially attacks grain boundaries, cell walls, and segregation-enriched melt-pool boundaries, creating grooves or relief that can be confused with pores and alter existing pore boundaries (pqac-00000042). In low-energy samples, etching can make pores "almost invisible" by modifying surrounding contrast, while in over-melted samples it can create corrosion trenches within melt pools that mimic voids (pqac-00000042). Therefore, porosity must be measured on unetched, polished surfaces first, followed by etching for microstructural examination.

**Etching recipes.** The following table summarizes reported conditions:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Which etchant is best for melt-pool boundaries?** Electrolytic 10% oxalic acid is the most widely used for LPBF 316L melt-pool boundary revelation, with conditions varying from 5 V / 90 s (pqac-00000031) to 15 V / 60 s depending on the laboratory. The voltage and time control the attack intensity: lower voltage/longer time gives gentler, more controlled revelation. Ronneberg et al. specifically noted good results at 5 V / 90 s for revealing both melt-pool boundaries and the cellular solidification structure (pqac-00000031). Mixed-acid reagent (HCl:acetic:HNO₃ = 3:2:1 by volume, 40–60 s immersion) was used by Vallejo et al. for detailed melt-pool and cellular analysis (pqac-00000034). Beraha II color etchant (10–30 s) was used by Mohr et al. for melt-pool depth determination and cell-size measurement (pqac-00000039). Aqua regia is aggressive and difficult to control for melt-pool boundary work. Kalling's No. 2 is mentioned by Krakhmalev et al. (doi:10.3390/met8080643) alongside electrolytic oxalic acid for LPBF 316L (pqac-00000036), but explicit comparative optimization was not reported.

**Strongly supported:** electrolytic 10% oxalic acid at room temperature is the most commonly reported and best-validated etchant for LPBF 316L melt-pool boundaries. **Weakly supported:** mixed-acid immersion and Beraha II are viable alternatives; glyceregia and Carpenter's are not represented in the retrieved LPBF 316L literature.

### 6. Measuring Last-Layer Melt-Pool Depth and Width

**Which pools count.** Mohr et al. (doi:10.1016/j.addma.2020.101080) measured melt-pool depths by analysing ten melt pools of the last exposed layer on etched cross-sections, using Part 4 (the upper 10 mm) at separation plane II, for each combination of parameters (275 W, 560–933 mm/s, 50 µm layer, 120 µm hatch, SLM280 HL) (pqac-00000039). Soares (2026) averaged eight measurements per single track for width and depth, with measurement uncertainty of approximately ±5–40 µm combining track-to-track variability and operator-dependent boundary identification (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). Vallejo et al. set the initial layer of the build so that the final top LPBF layer had no repeated laser melting, enabling clean measurement of melt-pool width and depth from that layer (pqac-00000033).

**Section angle distortion.** When a cross-section is cut at an angle θ to the scan direction, the apparent melt-pool width on the section is stretched by a factor of 1/cos(θ). For a 67° scan rotation between layers (common in LPBF), a longitudinal centreline section will be aligned with the scan direction of some layers and oblique to others. Schmid et al. (doi:10.1007/s40964-021-00173-7) noted that rotated scan directions (e.g., 67° between layers) make melt pools appear distorted and more difficult to analyse; they therefore used a 90° scan rotation for their automated melt-pool measurements (pqac-00000026). For the described thin walls (12.7 mm long, sectioned at mid-length), if the last-layer scan direction runs along the wall length, the centreline section is transverse to the scan tracks and shows their true depth and width. If the scan runs across the wall thickness (1.27 mm), the section is along the scan direction and reveals elongated melt-pool profiles; depth is still measurable but width is not. Measuring only pools whose scan direction is approximately perpendicular to the section plane (within ±15–20°) is advisable.

**How many pools to average.** Based on the literature, 8–10 melt pools from the last layer is the minimum for a reliable average (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000039). For a 12.7 mm long wall with 0.09 mm hatch spacing, the last layer contains ~140 tracks, so selecting 10–20 clearly resolved, non-edge pools is feasible. The measurement should exclude contour tracks (which use different parameters) and any pools at the wall ends where turn-around effects occur.

### 7. Realistic Hands-On Time

**Per mount (grinding and polishing).** The automated sequence in Table 3 (Westin et al.) totals approximately 27 minutes of machine time per batch of up to 6 samples (pqac-00000024). With cleaning between steps, sample inspection, and re-starts if needed, a realistic hands-on estimate is 45–60 minutes per batch including setup and cleanup. For 24 mounts in batches of 6, this is approximately 4 batches × 1 hour = 4–5 hours of polishing, plus cutting and mounting time (~20 min per mount for hot mounting, partially parallelisable). Total metallographic preparation: approximately 2–3 full working days for 24 mounts.

**Per SEM session.** Acquiring a stitched BSE mosaic of a ~10 mm² area at ~1 µm/pixel (comparable to the core analysis region of one wall) on a Thermo Fisher Apreo C requires approximately 15–30 minutes per wall section including setup, focus, and acquisition. With 7 walls per mount, one mount requires approximately 2–4 hours for porosity imaging. For 24 mounts, this represents approximately 48–96 hours of SEM time, or roughly 6–12 full 8-hour days of instrument time. Post-etching re-imaging for melt-pool depth (last layer only, smaller area) adds approximately 15–20 minutes per wall, or roughly 2 hours per mount for 7 walls. **Weakly supported:** these estimates are derived from procedure parameters rather than explicit time-motion studies.

### Summary of Key Artefacts That Bias Results

1. **Pore smearing during polishing** underestimates porosity by plastically closing small pores (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000045). Mitigation: adequate colloidal silica final polish; re-polish check; Archimedes or CT cross-validation.

2. **Pull-out** of loosely bonded particles (e.g., in lack-of-fusion regions) can create artificial voids that overestimate porosity. Using gentle polishing loads (20–30 N per sample) and diamond rather than alumina abrasives reduces this risk.

3. **Edge rounding** at the top of the thin wall reduces the measurable area for last-layer melt-pool depth and can cause apparent shallowing of pools. Edge retention by conductive epoxy mounting or electroless nickel plating before mounting is essential (pqac-00000023).

4. **Colloidal silica residue** can continue attacking the surface if not promptly removed, creating a "blurry white" appearance on ferrite and altering contrast (pqac-00000025). The final 30 seconds of the OP-S step should use water only (pqac-00000024).

5. **Section angle relative to scan direction** stretches the apparent melt-pool width by 1/cos(θ) (pqac-00000026). Only pools with scan direction approximately perpendicular to the section should be measured for width.

6. **2D stereological bias** means that a single cross-section systematically underestimates the true 3D pore volume for non-spherical pores and can make irregular pores appear more circular than their 3D shape (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000014).

7. **Etching artefacts** create grooves at melt-pool and cell boundaries that can be mistaken for pores if segmentation is applied to etched images (pqac-00000042). Porosity must always be measured before etching.

8. **Insufficient area** for image analysis at low porosity levels (≤0.1%) increases statistical uncertainty. At least several hundred mm² should be imaged at ~0.5% porosity; at 0.1%, more area or multiple sections are needed (pqac-00000031)."}

### 1. Cutting, Mounting, Grinding, and Polishing

**Cutting.** Cross-sections should be produced using precision diamond saws with water cooling or lubrication to minimize heat damage and surface deformation (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000002). Abrasive cut-off wheels, while faster, produce a wider kerf and more subsurface deformation; if used, they must be selected specifically for austenitic stainless steels and followed by sufficient grinding to remove the heat-affected zone (pqac-00000023). Wire-cutting (EDM) has also been used to extract sections more than 5 mm from build surfaces, with section thicknesses of approximately 2 mm (pqac-00000000). For the described thin-wall geometry (1.27 mm thick), precision diamond sawing is preferred because it produces a narrow kerf (~0.3–0.5 mm) with minimal subsurface deformation, which is critical when grinding must stop at a defined centreline plane. Protecting surfaces from clamping damage with rubber or metal shims is recommended (pqac-00000023).

**Conductive hot mounting and edge retention.** For SEM imaging, conductive mounts are essential. Westin et al. report positive experience with phenolic resin (PhenoCure™) and epoxy-based (EpoMet® G) mounting compounds (pqac-00000023). Cold-mount epoxies provide lower shrinkage and better edge retention for microstructure analysis but require several hours to cure and are softer, which may reduce polishing efficiency (pqac-00000023). For the top edge of a thin wall where melt-pool depth is measured in the last layer, edge retention is critical; conductive epoxy mounting or use of a nickel-plating or copper-plating technique before mounting can protect the edge from rounding during grinding and polishing. Chamfering or rounding of mount edges before grinding extends SiC paper and polishing cloth life (pqac-00000024).

**Grinding and polishing sequence.** The recommended automated preparation sequence, adapted from Westin et al. (doi:10.1007/s40194-025-02286-x, Tables 3–4) for 25 mm diameter embedded stainless steel specimens on a Struers Tegramin 30, is as follows:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

This protocol was developed for DED-arc stainless steel welds and AM deposits and has proven suitable for austenitic stainless steels with varying microstructures (pqac-00000024). Ronneberg et al. used a similar approach for LPBF 316L (200 W, 750 mm/s, 110 µm hatch, 50 µm layer, chessboard strategy on a Concept Laser): SiC grinding papers, diamond suspensions down to 1 µm, and final polishing with 0.06 µm (60 nm) colloidal silica suspension, followed by electrolytic etching (pqac-00000031). Vallejo et al. used SiC grinding papers and diamond paste polishing with a 0.05 µm colloidal silica final finish on LPBF 316L built on an SLM 125HL (200 W, 800 mm/s, 0.12 mm hatch, 0.03 mm layer) (pqac-00000034).

**Controlling material removal depth.** When grinding to a centreline plane, one approach is to mark the target plane with a permanent pen on the outer surface and account for expected grinding consumption (pqac-00000023). Inspection every 30 seconds during hand grinding—checking that the surface is flat, fully exposed, and free of misaligned scratches—is recommended (pqac-00000024). For automated preparation, the planar grinding step (SiC 500 or grinding stone) is repeated until all samples in the holder are planar before proceeding.

### 2. How Polishing Changes Measured Porosity

**Smearing.** Mechanical grinding and polishing can plastically deform metal over pore openings, partially or fully closing small voids and causing the measured porosity to underestimate the true value. This effect is widely recognized (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000045). Bahshwan (doi:10.3390/ma19214527) noted that "artifacts such as smeared pores can arise due to polishing" in LPBF 316L, though the magnitude was not quantified (pqac-00000045). Xavier et al. (doi:10.1007/s00170-019-04597-y) similarly noted that grinding and polishing "may affect the sizes and shapes of pores due to metal smearing" (pqac-00000030). Colloidal silica (OP-S) has a mild chemical–mechanical attack that helps remove the deformed layer, but over-polishing can create relief at phase boundaries and alter contrast (pqac-00000025).

**Comparison with X-ray CT and Archimedes.** Methods do not always agree, and the direction of discrepancy is not universal. In one LPBF 316L comparison by Zheng et al. (doi:10.3390/coatings11121562), optical metallography measured approximately 3.70% porosity, Archimedes gave 3.88%, and XCT yielded 3.00% for the same high-porosity sample, with the difference partly attributed to XCT's inability to resolve defects smaller than ~5 µm (pqac-00000009). In a low-porosity LPBF 316L study by Yusuf et al. (doi:10.3390/met7020064), Archimedes measured ~0.82% average porosity while XCT measured ~0.61% (pqac-00000010). Tajalli et al. (doi:10.1007/s13632-026-01349-9) compared OM, Archimedes, and XCT for 316L-2.5Cu and found close agreement for dense samples but divergence for samples with localized defect concentrations (pqac-00000008). XCT is generally considered more representative for three-dimensional pore characterization but has resolution limits; Archimedes provides only bulk density without pore-level information and is sensitive to surface defects (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006). **Strongly supported conclusion:** no single method is unbiased, and cross-validation is essential (pqac-00000007).

**Checking for artifacts.** Repeating the final polishing step and re-imaging can reveal whether apparent pore closure changes with additional material removal. Comparison with Archimedes density on the same specimen provides an independent bulk check. When feasible, CT scanning before sectioning provides a ground-truth reference (pqac-00000007).

### 3. Imaging Porosity: Optical vs. SEM BSE/SE, Magnification, Area, and Standards

**Imaging mode.** Ronneberg et al. used a Hirox RH-2000 digital microscope for porosity characterisation at a resolution of 2.61 µm/pixel and separately used a Hitachi S-3400N SEM with backscattered electron (BSE) detection at 13 kV accelerating voltage and ~8 mm working distance for microstructural examination of etched samples (pqac-00000031). BSE imaging on unetched, polished surfaces provides strong atomic-number contrast between the steel matrix and voids (appearing black), making segmentation straightforward. SE imaging also shows pores via topographic contrast but can be confused by polishing scratches. For the Thermo Fisher Apreo C (a field-emission SEM), BSE imaging at 10–15 kV is generally preferred for porosity because it provides flat, composition-sensitive contrast with minimal topographic noise.

**Magnification and pixel size.** Vallejo et al. used 100× optical magnification with five micrographs per section for porosity quantification (pqac-00000034). Ronneberg et al. used 2.61 µm/pixel and stitched mosaics covering at least 1000 mm² per section (pqac-00000031). For SEM, comparable coverage requires lower magnification (≤100×) with automated stage tiling and stitching. The minimum resolved pore size is fundamentally limited by the pixel size: Ronneberg et al. filtered out objects smaller than 25 µm² (< 4 pixels), corresponding to an equivalent circular diameter of ~5.6 µm (pqac-00000031). As a practical minimum, a pore should span at least 3–4 pixels in each direction to be reliably segmented.

**Area required for statistical significance.** Ronneberg et al. imaged >1000 mm² per section orientation for LPBF 316L at ~0.3–0.7% porosity to attain adequate statistics (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032). For the described thin walls (~1.27 × 7.6 mm cross-section = ~9.7 mm² per wall), the analysable core area (≥0.2 mm from faces, ≥1 mm from base and top) is roughly 0.87 × 5.6 mm ≈ 4.9 mm² per wall, so seven walls per mount ≈ 34 mm² of core area. At very low porosity (~0.1%), this small area may contain few pores, increasing statistical uncertainty. ASTM E1245 (doi:10.31399/asm.hb.v09.a0003789) specifies automatic image analysis of inclusions or phases with measurement of area fraction and uncertainty, requiring a sufficient number of fields to reduce the 95% confidence interval to an acceptable fraction of the measured value (pqac-00000047). **Weakly supported estimate:** for 0.1% porosity with ≤20% relative uncertainty, areas of several hundred mm² or more may be needed; at 1–5% porosity, tens of mm² can suffice (extrapolated from Ronneberg's practice of >1000 mm² for ~0.5% porosity).

**Number of sections per specimen.** Ronneberg et al. examined both horizontal and vertical sections for each build orientation to capture anisotropy and used the geometric mean of area-fraction porosity from two orthogonal sections to estimate volumetric relative density (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032). For the thin-wall geometry where a single lengthwise centreline section is taken, one section per wall is the minimum; repeating on a parallel section offset by ~0.3 mm would check for spatial variability.

### 4. Segmentation and Pore Classification

**Thresholding.** Grey-level thresholding is the standard approach. Mohr et al. used a fixed threshold of 136 (on an unspecified grey scale) for all cross-sections, applied via IMS Client software (pqac-00000039). Ronneberg et al. used ImageJ's "Analyse Particles" function (pqac-00000031). The PoreAnalyzer open-source tool (doi:10.3390/app11136086) and the RAPID tool (doi:10.3390/ma19214527) provide automated workflows for batch processing of optical micrographs with threshold tuning and morphological operators (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000045). Otsu's method or manual threshold selection with visual verification are common; the key is consistency across all images.

**Pore classification criteria.** The following table summarizes literature-derived heuristics for distinguishing lack-of-fusion (LoF), keyhole, and gas pores based on 2D (circularity, aspect ratio) and 3D (sphericity) shape descriptors:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

Key sources: Kan et al. (doi:10.1007/s10853-022-06990-7) describe gas pores as generally <100 µm and spherical, LoF pores as large and irregular, and keyhole pores as large and spherical (pqac-00000015). Nudelis and Mayr (doi:10.3390/met11121912) proposed a 3D CT-based classification using sphericity ≥0.6, compactness ≥0.4, and BB-factor ≥0.6 for spherical pores, with diameter classes of ≤100 µm, 100–200 µm, and >200 µm (pqac-00000012). Ellendt et al. (doi:10.3390/app11136086) used circularity ≥95% for gas pores and aspect ratio >5 for cracks in 2D optical analysis (pqac-00000016). These are heuristics rather than universal boundaries and should be validated for the specific process window.

### 5. Etching to Reveal Melt-Pool Boundaries

**Why porosity must be imaged before etching.** Chemical or electrolytic etching preferentially attacks grain boundaries, cell walls, and segregation-enriched melt-pool boundaries, creating grooves or relief that can be confused with pores and alter existing pore boundaries (pqac-00000042). In low-energy samples, etching can make pores "almost invisible" by modifying surrounding contrast, while in over-melted samples it can create corrosion trenches within melt pools that mimic voids (pqac-00000042). Therefore, porosity must be measured on unetched, polished surfaces first, followed by etching for microstructural examination.

**Etching recipes.** The following table summarizes reported conditions:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Which etchant is best for melt-pool boundaries?** Electrolytic 10% oxalic acid is the most widely used for LPBF 316L melt-pool boundary revelation, with conditions varying from 5 V / 90 s (pqac-00000031) to 15 V / 60 s depending on the laboratory. The voltage and time control the attack intensity: lower voltage/longer time gives gentler, more controlled revelation. Ronneberg et al. specifically noted good results at 5 V / 90 s for revealing both melt-pool boundaries and the cellular solidification structure (pqac-00000031). Mixed-acid reagent (HCl:acetic:HNO₃ = 3:2:1 by volume, 40–60 s immersion) was used by Vallejo et al. for detailed melt-pool and cellular analysis (pqac-00000034). Beraha II color etchant (10–30 s) was used by Mohr et al. for melt-pool depth determination and cell-size measurement (pqac-00000039). Aqua regia is aggressive and difficult to control for melt-pool boundary work. Kalling's No. 2 is mentioned by Krakhmalev et al. (doi:10.3390/met8080643) alongside electrolytic oxalic acid for LPBF 316L (pqac-00000036), but explicit comparative optimization was not reported.

**Strongly supported:** electrolytic 10% oxalic acid at room temperature is the most commonly reported and best-validated etchant for LPBF 316L melt-pool boundaries. **Weakly supported:** mixed-acid immersion and Beraha II are viable alternatives; glyceregia and Carpenter's are not represented in the retrieved LPBF 316L literature.

### 6. Measuring Last-Layer Melt-Pool Depth and Width

**Which pools count.** Mohr et al. (doi:10.1016/j.addma.2020.101080) measured melt-pool depths by analysing ten melt pools of the last exposed layer on etched cross-sections, using Part 4 (the upper 10 mm) at separation plane II, for each combination of parameters (275 W, 560–933 mm/s, 50 µm layer, 120 µm hatch, SLM280 HL) (pqac-00000039). Soares (2026) averaged eight measurements per single track for width and depth, with measurement uncertainty of approximately ±5–40 µm combining track-to-track variability and operator-dependent boundary identification (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). Vallejo et al. set the initial layer of the build so that the final top LPBF layer had no repeated laser melting, enabling clean measurement of melt-pool width and depth from that layer (pqac-00000033).

**Section angle distortion.** When a cross-section is cut at an angle θ to the scan direction, the apparent melt-pool width on the section is stretched by a factor of 1/cos(θ). For a 67° scan rotation between layers (common in LPBF), a longitudinal centreline section will be aligned with the scan direction of some layers and oblique to others. Schmid et al. (doi:10.1007/s40964-021-00173-7) noted that rotated scan directions (e.g., 67° between layers) make melt pools appear distorted and more difficult to analyse; they therefore used a 90° scan rotation for their automated melt-pool measurements (pqac-00000026). For the described thin walls (12.7 mm long, sectioned at mid-length), if the last-layer scan direction runs along the wall length, the centreline section is transverse to the scan tracks and shows their true depth and width. If the scan runs across the wall thickness (1.27 mm), the section is along the scan direction and reveals elongated melt-pool profiles; depth is still measurable but width is not. Measuring only pools whose scan direction is approximately perpendicular to the section plane (within ±15–20°) is advisable.

**How many pools to average.** Based on the literature, 8–10 melt pools from the last layer is the minimum for a reliable average (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000039). For a 12.7 mm long wall with 0.09 mm hatch spacing, the last layer contains ~140 tracks, so selecting 10–20 clearly resolved, non-edge pools is feasible. The measurement should exclude contour tracks (which use different parameters) and any pools at the wall ends where turn-around effects occur.

### 7. Realistic Hands-On Time

**Per mount (grinding and polishing).** The automated sequence in Table 3 (Westin et al.) totals approximately 27 minutes of machine time per batch of up to 6 samples (pqac-00000024). With cleaning between steps, sample inspection, and re-starts if needed, a realistic hands-on estimate is 45–60 minutes per batch including setup and cleanup. For 24 mounts in batches of 6, this is approximately 4 batches × 1 hour = 4–5 hours of polishing, plus cutting and mounting time (~20 min per mount for hot mounting, partially parallelisable). Total metallographic preparation: approximately 2–3 full working days for 24 mounts.

**Per SEM session.** Acquiring a stitched BSE mosaic of a ~10 mm² area at ~1 µm/pixel (comparable to the core analysis region of one wall) on a Thermo Fisher Apreo C requires approximately 15–30 minutes per wall section including setup, focus, and acquisition. With 7 walls per mount, one mount requires approximately 2–4 hours for porosity imaging. For 24 mounts, this represents approximately 48–96 hours of SEM time, or roughly 6–12 full 8-hour days of instrument time. Post-etching re-imaging for melt-pool depth (last layer only, smaller area) adds approximately 15–20 minutes per wall, or roughly 2 hours per mount for 7 walls. **Weakly supported:** these estimates are derived from procedure parameters rather than explicit time-motion studies.

### Summary of Key Artefacts That Bias Results

1. **Pore smearing during polishing** underestimates porosity by plastically closing small pores (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000045). Mitigation: adequate colloidal silica final polish; re-polish check; Archimedes or CT cross-validation.

2. **Pull-out** of loosely bonded particles (e.g., in lack-of-fusion regions) can create artificial voids that overestimate porosity. Using gentle polishing loads (20–30 N per sample) and diamond rather than alumina abrasives reduces this risk.

3. **Edge rounding** at the top of the thin wall reduces the measurable area for last-layer melt-pool depth and can cause apparent shallowing of pools. Edge retention by conductive epoxy mounting or electroless nickel plating before mounting is essential (pqac-00000023).

4. **Colloidal silica residue** can continue attacking the surface if not promptly removed, creating a "blurry white" appearance on ferrite and altering contrast (pqac-00000025). The final 30 seconds of the OP-S step should use water only (pqac-00000024).

5. **Section angle relative to scan direction** stretches the apparent melt-pool width by 1/cos(θ) (pqac-00000026). Only pools with scan direction approximately perpendicular to the section should be measured for width.

6. **2D stereological bias** means that a single cross-section systematically underestimates the true 3D pore volume for non-spherical pores and can make irregular pores appear more circular than their 3D shape (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000014).

7. **Etching artefacts** create grooves at melt-pool and cell boundaries that can be mistaken for pores if segmentation is applied to etched images (pqac-00000042). Porosity must always be measured before etching.

8. **Insufficient area** for image analysis at low porosity levels (≤0.1%) increases statistical uncertainty. At least several hundred mm² should be imaged at ~0.5% porosity; at 0.1%, more area or multiple sections are needed (pqac-00000031)."}

What is the best practice for preparing and imaging cross-sections of LPBF 316L thin walls to measure porosity and last-layer melt-pool depth in an SEM, and which artefacts bias the results? Context: laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M, L-PBF) of commercial gas-atomized 316L stainless steel powder (about 15-45 um) on a Concept Laser M2 cusing (CL WRX Control 2.4; two 400 W class continuous-wave Yb fibre lasers at about 1070 nm, only one used; galvanometer scanner; nitrogen or argon; no plate heating; layer thickness 30 or 50 um, not yet confirmed). The machine's production 316L parameter set uses, for the core hatch, 370 W, 1350 mm/s, 0.09 mm hatch spacing and a 130 um spot (P/v = 0.274 J/mm), contours at 100-120 W and 130-220 mm/s with a 50-70 um spot, and an upskin at 200 W, 980 mm/s, 0.075 mm hatch. Every wall has its own core and upskin laser power P and scan speed v (contours unchanged): 60 settings from a scrambled Sobol sequence over P = 150-370 W and P/v = 0.09-0.55 J/mm (v about 335-2930 mm/s; about 33-204 J/mm^3 at 30 um layers), plus the production hatch as a control. Three parts stand on each of four removable 88 mm square 316L panels; the fourth panel is turned 90 degrees so its walls run across the recoater instead of along it, and repeats 18 settings and the control, giving 21 pairs printed in both orientations. After the build each part is cut lengthwise near its centreline and between walls 4 and 5, hot-mounted in 1.25 in conductive mounts, ground to the centreline (a section through every wall's thickness and height at mid-length), polished, imaged unetched in an SEM (Thermo Fisher Apreo C) for porosity in each wall's core (at least 0.2 mm from the faces, 1 mm from the base and the top), then etched to reveal the last layer's melt-pool boundaries. The results will be compared with the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module (CALPHAD-based properties; steady-state and transient melt-pool calculations; printability maps of lack of fusion, keyholing and balling), to calibrate and test it, and later builds will choose settings by batch Bayesian optimization.

Cutting (abrasive cut-off versus precision diamond saws; kerf; heat damage), conductive hot mounting and edge retention at the top of a wall, and the grinding and polishing sequence for 316L (SiC grits, diamond, colloidal silica or alumina, times and loads), including how much material to remove to reach a plane and how to stop at it.

Imaging porosity: optical versus SEM BSE versus SE; magnification and pixel size; the smallest pore that should be counted; stitched mosaics; how large an area is needed for a given uncertainty at 0.1%, 1% and 5% porosity (ASTM E1245, E2109, ISO/ASTM 52900 family), and how many sections per specimen.
4. Segmentation and classification: thresholding methods; classifying lack-of-fusion, keyhole and gas pores by size, circularity and aspect ratio, with the thresholds used.
5. Etching 316L to reveal melt-pool boundaries and the cellular structure for SEM and optical imaging (electrolytic oxalic acid, aqua regia, Kalling's no. 2, glyceregia, V2A-Beize, Carpenter's): recipes, times, which works best for melt-pool boundaries, and why porosity must be imaged before etching.
6. Measuring the last layer's melt-pool depth and width in a section through a wall: which pools count, how the section angle to the scan direction distorts them, and how many pools to average.
7. Realistic hands-on time per mount and per SEM image for a set of about 24 mounts.

## Best Practice for Preparing and Imaging Cross-Sections of LPBF 316L Thin Walls: Porosity and Melt-Pool Depth Measurement by SEM

### 1. Cutting, Mounting, Grinding, and Polishing

**Cutting.** Cross-sections should be produced using precision diamond saws with water cooling or lubrication to minimize heat damage and surface deformation (westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 4-5, sala2025theroleof pages 4-5). Abrasive cut-off wheels, while faster, produce a wider kerf and more subsurface deformation; if used, they must be selected specifically for austenitic stainless steels and followed by sufficient grinding to remove the heat-affected zone (westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 4-5). Wire-cutting (EDM) has also been used to extract sections more than 5 mm from build surfaces, with section thicknesses of approximately 2 mm (zheng2021defectanalysisof pages 4-6). For the described thin-wall geometry (1.27 mm thick), precision diamond sawing is preferred because it produces a narrow kerf (~0.3–0.5 mm) with minimal subsurface deformation, which is critical when grinding must stop at a defined centreline plane. Protecting surfaces from clamping damage with rubber or metal shims is recommended (westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 4-5).

**Conductive hot mounting and edge retention.** For SEM imaging, conductive mounts are essential. Westin et al. report positive experience with phenolic resin (PhenoCure™) and epoxy-based (EpoMet® G) mounting compounds (westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 4-5). Cold-mount epoxies provide lower shrinkage and better edge retention for microstructure analysis but require several hours to cure and are softer, which may reduce polishing efficiency (westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 4-5). For the top edge of a thin wall where melt-pool depth is measured in the last layer, edge retention is critical; conductive epoxy mounting or use of a nickel-plating or copper-plating technique before mounting can protect the edge from rounding during grinding and polishing. Chamfering or rounding of mount edges before grinding extends SiC paper and polishing cloth life (westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 7-9).

**Grinding and polishing sequence.** The recommended automated preparation sequence, adapted from Westin et al. (doi:10.1007/s40194-025-02286-x, Tables 3–4) for 25 mm diameter embedded stainless steel specimens on a Struers Tegramin 30, is as follows:

| Step | Surface/Abrasive | Suspension/Lubricant | Time (min) | Load per sample (N) | Platen speed (rpm) | Sample-holder speed (rpm) |
|---:|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | SiC P500 paper | Water | 2:00 | 40 | 300 | 150 |
| 2 | SiC P1000 paper | Water | 2:00 | 35 | 300 | 150 |
| 3 | SiC P2000 paper | Water | 2:30 | 30 | 300 | 150 |
| 4 | DP-Mol cloth | DiaDuo-2, 3 µm diamond | 5:00 | 30 | 250 | 150 |
| 5 | DP-Dac cloth | DiaDuo-2, 1 µm diamond | 6:30 | 25 | 250 | 150 |
| 6 | MD-Chem cloth | OP-S NonDry colloidal silica; use water only for the final 0:30 to remove residual silica | 9:00 | 20 | 200 | 150 |
| Note | Prompt post-polish cleaning | Rinse immediately so residual silica does not continue attacking the surface; validate on sacrificial LPBF 316L mounts for pore smearing, pull-out, edge retention, and relief. | — | — | — | — |
| Source | Westin et al., Table 3 and §4.6 (westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 7-9, westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 9-10) | Optimized automated sequence for embedded 25 mm stainless-steel specimens | — | — | — | — |


*Table: Recommended automated preparation sequence from SiC P500 through colloidal silica for mounted LPBF 316L cross-sections. The final water-only interval removes residual silica that could continue attacking the polished surface.*

This protocol was developed for DED-arc stainless steel welds and AM deposits and has proven suitable for austenitic stainless steels with varying microstructures (westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 7-9). Ronneberg et al. used a similar approach for LPBF 316L (200 W, 750 mm/s, 110 µm hatch, 50 µm layer, chessboard strategy on a Concept Laser): SiC grinding papers, diamond suspensions down to 1 µm, and final polishing with 0.06 µm (60 nm) colloidal silica suspension, followed by electrolytic etching (ronneberg2020revealingrelationshipsbetween pages 2-3). **Smearing.** Mechanical grinding and polishing can plastically deform metal over pore openings, partially or fully closing small voids and causing the measured porosity to underestimate the true value. **Thresholding.** Grey-level thresholding is the standard approach. Mohr et al. used a fixed threshold of 136 (on an unspecified grey scale) for all cross-sections, applied via IMS Client software (mohr2020effectsofinter pages 4-6). Ronneberg et al. used ImageJ's "Analyse Particles" function (ronneberg2020revealingrelationshipsbetween pages 2-3). The PoreAnalyzer open-source tool (doi:10.3390/app11136086) and the RAPID tool (doi:10.3390/ma19214527) provide automated workflows for batch processing of optical micrographs with threshold tuning and morphological operators (ellendt2021poreanalyzer—anopensourceframework pages 2-4, bahshwan2026fastcharacterizationof pages 1-3). **Why porosity must be imaged before etching.** Chemical or electrolytic etching preferentially attacks grain boundaries, cell walls, and segregation-enriched melt-pool boundaries, creating grooves or relief that can be confused with pores and alter existing pore boundaries (zheng2021defectanalysisof pages 10-14). In low-energy samples, etching can make pores "almost invisible" by modifying surrounding contrast, while in over-melted samples it can create corrosion trenches within melt pools that mimic voids (zheng2021defectanalysisof pages 10-14). ### 6. Measuring Last-Layer Melt-Pool Depth and Width

**Which pools count.** Mohr et al.
