Vallejo et al. set the initial layer of the build so that the final top LPBF layer had no repeated laser melting, enabling clean measurement of melt-pool width and depth from that layer (vallejo2021processoptimizationand pages 2-4).

**Section angle distortion.** When a cross-section is cut at an angle θ to the scan direction, the apparent melt-pool width on the section is stretched by a factor of 1/cos(θ). For a 67° scan rotation between layers (common in LPBF), a longitudinal centreline section will be aligned with the scan direction of some layers and oblique to others. Schmid et al. (doi:10.1007/s40964-021-00173-7) noted that rotated scan directions (e.g., 67° between layers) make melt pools appear distorted and more difficult to analyse; they therefore used a 90° scan rotation for their automated melt-pool measurements (schmid2021anewapproach pages 1-3). For the described thin walls (12.7 mm long, sectioned at mid-length), if the last-layer scan direction runs along the wall length, the centreline section is transverse to the scan tracks and shows their true depth and width. If the scan runs across the wall thickness (1.27 mm), the section is along the scan direction and reveals elongated melt-pool profiles; depth is still measurable but width is not. Measuring only pools whose scan direction is approximately perpendicular to the section plane (within ±15–20°) is advisable.

**How many pools to average.** Based on the literature, 8–10 melt pools from the last layer is the minimum for a reliable average (soares2026processoptimizationofa pages 81-86, mohr2020effectsofinter pages 4-6). For a 12.7 mm long wall with 0.09 mm hatch spacing, the last layer contains ~140 tracks, so selecting 10–20 clearly resolved, non-edge pools is feasible. The measurement should exclude contour tracks (which use different parameters) and any pools at the wall ends where turn-around effects occur.

### 7. Realistic Hands-On Time

**Per mount (grinding and polishing).** The automated sequence in Table 3 (Westin et al.) totals approximately 27 minutes of machine time per batch of up to 6 samples (westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 7-9). With cleaning between steps, sample inspection, and re-starts if needed, a realistic hands-on estimate is 45–60 minutes per batch including setup and cleanup. For 24 mounts in batches of 6, this is approximately 4 batches × 1 hour = 4–5 hours of polishing, plus cutting and mounting time (~20 min per mount for hot mounting, partially parallelisable). Total metallographic preparation: approximately 2–3 full working days for 24 mounts.

**Per SEM session.** Acquiring a stitched BSE mosaic of a ~10 mm² area at ~1 µm/pixel (comparable to the core analysis region of one wall) on a Thermo Fisher Apreo C requires approximately 15–30 minutes per wall section including setup, focus, and acquisition. With 7 walls per mount, one mount requires approximately 2–4 hours for porosity imaging. For 24 mounts, this represents approximately 48–96 hours of SEM time, or roughly 6–12 full 8-hour days of instrument time. Post-etching re-imaging for melt-pool depth (last layer only, smaller area) adds approximately 15–20 minutes per wall, or roughly 2 hours per mount for 7 walls. **Weakly supported:** these estimates are derived from procedure parameters rather than explicit time-motion studies.

### Summary of Key Artefacts That Bias Results

1. **Pore smearing during polishing** underestimates porosity by plastically closing small pores (kan2022acriticalreview pages 1-3, bahshwan2026fastcharacterizationof pages 1-3). Mitigation: adequate colloidal silica final polish; re-polish check; Archimedes or CT cross-validation.

2. **Pull-out** of loosely bonded particles (e.g., in lack-of-fusion regions) can create artificial voids that overestimate porosity. Using gentle polishing loads (20–30 N per sample) and diamond rather than alumina abrasives reduces this risk.

3. **Edge rounding** at the top of the thin wall reduces the measurable area for last-layer melt-pool depth and can cause apparent shallowing of pools. Edge retention by conductive epoxy mounting or electroless nickel plating before mounting is essential (westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 4-5).

4. **Colloidal silica residue** can continue attacking the surface if not promptly removed, creating a "blurry white" appearance on ferrite and altering contrast (westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 9-10). The final 30 seconds of the OP-S step should use water only (westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 7-9).

5. **Section angle relative to scan direction** stretches the apparent melt-pool width by 1/cos(θ) (schmid2021anewapproach pages 1-3). Only pools with scan direction approximately perpendicular to the section should be measured for width.

6. **2D stereological bias** means that a single cross-section systematically underestimates the true 3D pore volume for non-spherical pores and can make irregular pores appear more circular than their 3D shape (cerezo2024tomographyoflaser pages 7-9).

7. **Etching artefacts** create grooves at melt-pool and cell boundaries that can be mistaken for pores if segmentation is applied to etched images (zheng2021defectanalysisof pages 10-14). Porosity must always be measured before etching.

8. **Insufficient area** for image analysis at low porosity levels (≤0.1%) increases statistical uncertainty. At least several hundred mm² should be imaged at ~0.5% porosity; at 0.1%, more area or multiple sections are needed (ronneberg2020revealingrelationshipsbetween pages 2-3).

For the described thin walls (~1.27 × 7.6 mm cross-section = ~9.7 mm² per wall), the analysable core area (≥0.2 mm from faces, ≥1 mm from base and top) is roughly 0.87 × 5.6 mm ≈ 4.9 mm² per wall, so seven walls per mount ≈ 34 mm² of core area. At very low porosity (~0.1%), this small area may contain few pores, increasing statistical uncertainty. ASTM E1245 (doi:10.31399/asm.hb.v09.a0003789) specifies automatic image analysis of inclusions or phases with measurement of area fraction and uncertainty, requiring a sufficient number of fields to reduce the 95% confidence interval to an acceptable fraction of the measured value (pqac-00000047). **Weakly supported estimate:** for 0.1% porosity with ≤20% relative uncertainty, areas of several hundred mm² or more may be needed; at 1–5% porosity, tens of mm² can suffice (extrapolated from Ronneberg's practice of >1000 mm² for ~0.5% porosity).

**Number of sections per specimen.** Ronneberg et al. examined both horizontal and vertical sections for each build orientation to capture anisotropy and used the geometric mean of area-fraction porosity from two orthogonal sections to estimate volumetric relative density (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032). For the thin-wall geometry where a single lengthwise centreline section is taken, one section per wall is the minimum; repeating on a parallel section offset by ~0.3 mm would check for spatial variability.

### 4. Segmentation and Pore Classification

**Thresholding.** Grey-level thresholding is the standard approach. Mohr et al. used a fixed threshold of 136 (on an unspecified grey scale) for all cross-sections, applied via IMS Client software (pqac-00000039). Ronneberg et al. used ImageJ's "Analyse Particles" function (pqac-00000031). The PoreAnalyzer open-source tool (doi:10.3390/app11136086) and the RAPID tool (doi:10.3390/ma19214527) provide automated workflows for batch processing of optical micrographs with threshold tuning and morphological operators (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000045). Otsu's method or manual threshold selection with visual verification are common; the key is consistency across all images.

**Pore classification criteria.** The following table summarizes literature-derived heuristics for distinguishing lack-of-fusion (LoF), keyhole, and gas pores based on 2D (circularity, aspect ratio) and 3D (sphericity) shape descriptors:

| Pore Type | Typical Size | Circularity (2D) | Aspect Ratio | Sphericity (3D) | Morphology Description | Source(s) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Gas | Typically <100 µm | ≥0.95 in one classifier | High, near 1; 0.65 reported in one study | Typically ≥0.6 | Small, nearly spherical voids associated with trapped gas; mean Feret diameter ≈0.05 mm and aspect ratio 0.65 in one dataset. | (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018) |
| Keyhole | Commonly 100–500+ µm, but may overlap gas-pore sizes | Moderate to high | Moderate; approximately 0.5–0.8, with 0.57 reported in one study | Moderate; approximately 0.4–0.6 | Round, spherical, or semispherical pores produced by collapse of a vapor depression; mean Feret diameter ≈0.09 mm and aspect ratio 0.57 in one dataset. | (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018) |
| Lack of fusion | Commonly 100–500+ µm | Low; often <0.5 | Low when defined as minor/major axis; often <0.5 | Typically <0.4 | Large, irregular, flattened, or elongated defects between tracks or layers, frequently containing unmelted powder; mean Feret diameter ≈0.26 mm and aspect ratio 0.33 in one dataset. | (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019) |


*Table: Morphology-based criteria for distinguishing gas, keyhole, and lack-of-fusion pores. The thresholds are literature-specific heuristics rather than universal mechanistic boundaries.*

Key sources: Kan et al. (doi:10.1007/s10853-022-06990-7) describe gas pores as generally <100 µm and spherical, LoF pores as large and irregular, and keyhole pores as large and spherical (pqac-00000015). Nudelis and Mayr (doi:10.3390/met11121912) proposed a 3D CT-based classification using sphericity ≥0.6, compactness ≥0.4, and BB-factor ≥0.6 for spherical pores, with diameter classes of ≤100 µm, 100–200 µm, and >200 µm (pqac-00000012). Ellendt et al. (doi:10.3390/app11136086) used circularity ≥95% for gas pores and aspect ratio >5 for cracks in 2D optical analysis (pqac-00000016). These are heuristics rather than universal boundaries and should be validated for the specific process window.

### 5. Etching to Reveal Melt-Pool Boundaries

**Why porosity must be imaged before etching.** Chemical or electrolytic etching preferentially attacks grain boundaries, cell walls, and segregation-enriched melt-pool boundaries, creating grooves or relief that can be confused with pores and alter existing pore boundaries (pqac-00000042). In low-energy samples, etching can make pores "almost invisible" by modifying surrounding contrast, while in over-melted samples it can create corrosion trenches within melt pools that mimic voids (pqac-00000042). Therefore, porosity must be measured on unetched, polished surfaces first, followed by etching for microstructural examination.

**Etching recipes.** The following table summarizes reported conditions:

| Etchant Name | Composition | Method | Voltage/Current | Time (s) | Temperature | Best For | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Electrolytic oxalic acid (Rønneberg 2020) | 10% oxalic-acid solution | Electrolytic | 5 V | 90 | Room temperature | Melt-pool boundaries and cellular structure for optical microscopy and SEM | Rønneberg et al., 2020 (pqac-00000031) |
| Electrolytic oxalic acid (Sangoi 2025) | 10% saturated oxalic acid | Electrolytic | 12 V | 90 | Room temperature | General microstructure and SEM/EBSD preparation; not explicitly optimized for melt-pool boundaries | Sangoi et al., 2025 (pqac-00000021) |
| Electrolytic oxalic acid (Vukkum 2026) | 10% oxalic acid | Electrolytic | 15 V | 60 | Room temperature | Melt-pool and cellular microstructure | Vukkum et al., 2026; condition reported in retrieved source text |
| Mixed-acid reagent (Vallejo 2021) | HCl:acetic acid:HNO₃ = 3:2:1 by volume | Immersion | N/A | 40–60 | Room temperature | Detailed melt-pool-boundary and cellular-structure analysis | Vallejo et al., 2021 (pqac-00000034) |
| Aqua regia | HNO₃:HCl = 1:3 by volume | Immersion | N/A | Seconds; stop by visual endpoint | Room temperature | General 316/316L microstructure; comparatively aggressive and prone to relief if overetched | Chabak et al., 2021 (pqac-00000001) |
| Beraha II | Color etchant; exact formulation not reported in the retrieved passage | Immersion | N/A | 10–30 | Room temperature | Melt-pool contrast and subgrain/cell-size examination | Mohr et al., 2020 (pqac-00000039) |
| V2A-Beize | Proprietary/formulation not reported in the retrieved passage | Chemical immersion | N/A | 20 | Room temperature only; 50 °C caused overetching, stains, or large holes | General steel microstructure; evidence is from Fe–9%Cr ODS steel rather than LPBF 316L | Cavaliere, 2019 (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022) |


*Table: Reported etching conditions for revealing LPBF 316L melt-pool or cellular features, with limitations flagged where the retrieved evidence used another steel or did not establish optimization for melt-pool boundaries.*

**Which etchant is best for melt-pool boundaries?** Electrolytic 10% oxalic acid is the most widely used for LPBF 316L melt-pool boundary revelation, with conditions varying from 5 V / 90 s (pqac-00000031) to 15 V / 60 s depending on the laboratory. The voltage and time control the attack intensity: lower voltage/longer time gives gentler, more controlled revelation. Ronneberg et al. specifically noted good results at 5 V / 90 s for revealing both melt-pool boundaries and the cellular solidification structure (pqac-00000031). Mixed-acid reagent (HCl:acetic:HNO₃ = 3:2:1 by volume, 40–60 s immersion) was used by Vallejo et al. for detailed melt-pool and cellular analysis (pqac-00000034). Beraha II color etchant (10–30 s) was used by Mohr et al. for melt-pool depth determination and cell-size measurement (pqac-00000039). Aqua regia is aggressive and difficult to control for melt-pool boundary work. Kalling's No. 2 is mentioned by Krakhmalev et al. (doi:10.3390/met8080643) alongside electrolytic oxalic acid for LPBF 316L (pqac-00000036), but explicit comparative optimization was not reported.

**Strongly supported:** electrolytic 10% oxalic acid at room temperature is the most commonly reported and best-validated etchant for LPBF 316L melt-pool boundaries. **Weakly supported:** mixed-acid immersion and Beraha II are viable alternatives; glyceregia and Carpenter's are not represented in the retrieved LPBF 316L literature.

### 6. Measuring Last-Layer Melt-Pool Depth and Width

**Which pools count.** Mohr et al. (doi:10.1016/j.addma.2020.101080) measured melt-pool depths by analysing ten melt pools of the last exposed layer on etched cross-sections, using Part 4 (the upper 10 mm) at separation plane II, for each combination of parameters (275 W, 560–933 mm/s, 50 µm layer, 120 µm hatch, SLM280 HL) (pqac-00000039). Soares (2026) averaged eight measurements per single track for width and depth, with measurement uncertainty of approximately ±5–40 µm combining track-to-track variability and operator-dependent boundary identification (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). Vallejo et al. set the initial layer of the build so that the final top LPBF layer had no repeated laser melting, enabling clean measurement of melt-pool width and depth from that layer (pqac-00000033).

**Section angle distortion.** When a cross-section is cut at an angle θ to the scan direction, the apparent melt-pool width on the section is stretched by a factor of 1/cos(θ). For a 67° scan rotation between layers (common in LPBF), a longitudinal centreline section will be aligned with the scan direction of some layers and oblique to others. Schmid et al. (doi:10.1007/s40964-021-00173-7) noted that rotated scan directions (e.g., 67° between layers) make melt pools appear distorted and more difficult to analyse; they therefore used a 90° scan rotation for their automated melt-pool measurements (pqac-00000026). For the described thin walls (12.7 mm long, sectioned at mid-length), if the last-layer scan direction runs along the wall length, the centreline section is transverse to the scan tracks and shows their true depth and width. If the scan runs across the wall thickness (1.27 mm), the section is along the scan direction and reveals elongated melt-pool profiles; depth is still measurable but width is not. Measuring only pools whose scan direction is approximately perpendicular to the section plane (within ±15–20°) is advisable.

**How many pools to average.** Based on the literature, 8–10 melt pools from the last layer is the minimum for a reliable average (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000039). For a 12.7 mm long wall with 0.09 mm hatch spacing, the last layer contains ~140 tracks, so selecting 10–20 clearly resolved, non-edge pools is feasible. The measurement should exclude contour tracks (which use different parameters) and any pools at the wall ends where turn-around effects occur.

### 7. Realistic Hands-On Time

**Per mount (grinding and polishing).** The automated sequence in Table 3 (Westin et al.) totals approximately 27 minutes of machine time per batch of up to 6 samples (pqac-00000024). With cleaning between steps, sample inspection, and re-starts if needed, a realistic hands-on estimate is 45–60 minutes per batch including setup and cleanup. For 24 mounts in batches of 6, this is approximately 4 batches × 1 hour = 4–5 hours of polishing, plus cutting and mounting time (~20 min per mount for hot mounting, partially parallelisable). Total metallographic preparation: approximately 2–3 full working days for 24 mounts.

**Per SEM session.** Acquiring a stitched BSE mosaic of a ~10 mm² area at ~1 µm/pixel (comparable to the core analysis region of one wall) on a Thermo Fisher Apreo C requires approximately 15–30 minutes per wall section including setup, focus, and acquisition. With 7 walls per mount, one mount requires approximately 2–4 hours for porosity imaging. For 24 mounts, this represents approximately 48–96 hours of SEM time, or roughly 6–12 full 8-hour days of instrument time. Post-etching re-imaging for melt-pool depth (last layer only, smaller area) adds approximately 15–20 minutes per wall, or roughly 2 hours per mount for 7 walls. **Weakly supported:** these estimates are derived from procedure parameters rather than explicit time-motion studies.

### Summary of Key Artefacts That Bias Results

1. **Pore smearing during polishing** underestimates porosity by plastically closing small pores (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000045). Mitigation: adequate colloidal silica final polish; re-polish check; Archimedes or CT cross-validation.

2. **Pull-out** of loosely bonded particles (e.g., in lack-of-fusion regions) can create artificial voids that overestimate porosity. Using gentle polishing loads (20–30 N per sample) and diamond rather than alumina abrasives reduces this risk.

3. **Edge rounding** at the top of the thin wall reduces the measurable area for last-layer melt-pool depth and can cause apparent shallowing of pools. Edge retention by conductive epoxy mounting or electroless nickel plating before mounting is essential (pqac-00000023).

4. **Colloidal silica residue** can continue attacking the surface if not promptly removed, creating a "blurry white" appearance on ferrite and altering contrast (pqac-00000025). The final 30 seconds of the OP-S step should use water only (pqac-00000024).

5. **Section angle relative to scan direction** stretches the apparent melt-pool width by 1/cos(θ) (pqac-00000026). Only pools with scan direction approximately perpendicular to the section should be measured for width.

6. **2D stereological bias** means that a single cross-section systematically underestimates the true 3D pore volume for non-spherical pores and can make irregular pores appear more circular than their 3D shape (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000014).

7. **Etching artefacts** create grooves at melt-pool and cell boundaries that can be mistaken for pores if segmentation is applied to etched images (pqac-00000042). Porosity must always be measured before etching.

8. **Insufficient area** for image analysis at low porosity levels (≤0.1%) increases statistical uncertainty. At least several hundred mm² should be imaged at ~0.5% porosity; at 0.1%, more area or multiple sections are needed (pqac-00000031).

It does, however, identify the methodological limitation behind optical microscopy (OM): OM characterizes pores on a polished two-dimensional surface, whereas X-ray computed tomography (CT) evaluates the full three-dimensional pore volume. A 2D section can cut through a pore in a way that makes it appear more circular and uniform, while the unmeasured third dimension hides pore non-uniformity. Consequently, 3D CT provides a broader and more precise assessment of pore dimensions and shape, including more reliable maximum and minimum pore sizes. In the 18Ni300 LPBF sample, CT measured relative porosity below 0.1% throughout the construction axis, corresponding to relative density above 99.9%, including surface porosity. OM measurements reported porosity as high as 0.185% of the examined section, indicating that the optical result was higher than the CT result in this study. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies limitations relevant to comparing porosity measurements in LPBF alloys, although it does not specifically explain the pore-smearing mechanism caused by metallographic polishing. Optical microscopy (OM) requires cutting and polishing, making it destructive, and examines a fundamentally two-dimensional section. Consequently, it is more susceptible to selection bias: pores may be missed depending on the section, while preparation-related deformation or smearing could further obscure pore boundaries and reduce the apparent measured porosity. X-ray computed tomography (X-ray CT) is described as a non-destructive three-dimensional method and can analyze the pore population more representatively. However, CT accuracy depends on the trade-off among pore-size resolution, analyzed volume, and cost; inadequate resolution can itself cause porosity underestimation, and filtering for noise may reduce image clarity. For a given sample volume, the cited study found CT generally more cost-effective and accurate than OM. Archimedes density measurement is also non-destructive, but is less accurate for nearly fully dense parts because the true theoretical alloy density may be uncertain and the measurement can be affected by other factors. Thus, OM may report lower or more variable porosity than CT, while Archimedes provides a bulk estimate with distinct accuracy limitations.
contexts.question: How does metallographic polishing cause pore smearing that underestimates porosity in LPBF metals, and how does measured porosity from optical microscopy compare with X-ray CT and Archimedes density measurements?

For optical microscopy (OM), sections were mechanically polished to a mirror finish and pores were measured in two-dimensional cross-sections by pixel counting in FIJI; circularity was also calculated from each pore’s perimeter and area. Mechanical polishing can smear or plastically deform the edges of small, shallow, or partially open pores, potentially closing voids or making them appear smaller in the polished section, thereby underestimating porosity. OM also samples only selected planes, so it may miss pores between sections and cannot directly measure their full three-dimensional volume. X-ray CT instead reconstructs internal defects in 3D and calculates porosity or relative density from pore volumes, while applying a detection threshold: pores smaller than five voxels were removed and the smallest detectable equivalent pore diameter was 4.5 µm. Thus, CT should generally provide a more representative porosity value than polished-section OM, especially for irregular and subsurface pores, although its resolution limits detection of the smallest defects. The excerpt does not provide the Archimedes results or quantify the differences among OM, CT, and Archimedes measurements.
contexts.question: How does metallographic polishing cause pore smearing that underestimates porosity in LPBF metals, and how does measured porosity from optical microscopy compare with X-ray CT and Archimedes density measurements?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an X-ray/CT-based LPBF pore classification scheme that combines maximum pore diameter, multiple shape descriptors, and pore location. Shape is evaluated using sphericity (the surface-area ratio relative to an equal-volume sphere), compactness (pore volume relative to a sphere defined by the maximum pore radius), and the bounding-box factor (BB factor), defined as the shortest pore dimension divided by the longest dimension (S/L). Spherical pores satisfy compactness Ω ≥ 0.4, sphericity Ψ ≥ 0.6, and BB factor ≥ 0.6; irregular pores have Ω < 0.4, Ψ < 0.6, and BB factor in [0, 1]. Diameter classes are A/D: ≤100 µm, B/E: >100 to ≤200 µm, and C/F: >200 µm, with A-C spherical and D-F irregular. Location further distinguishes internal pores (a/h < 0.8) from near-surface pores (a/h > 0.8). The passage states that combining diameter and shape enables classification of hydrogen-induced (gas), keyhole, and lack-of-fusion pores, but it does not provide an explicit one-to-one mapping of those pore mechanisms to circularity, aspect-ratio, or individual classes. It also emphasizes that all three shape indicators are needed to minimize misclassification.
contexts.question: What are the pore classification criteria for LPBF: how to distinguish lack-of-fusion pores, keyhole pores, and gas pores using circularity, aspect ratio, size thresholds, and shape descriptors?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a morphology-based LPBF defect classification using image segmentation, circularity, aspect ratio, object hierarchy, and circle-equivalent diameter. Circularity is calculated as CD = 4πA/P² from defect area and perimeter; gas pores are classified when circularity is at least 95%, reflecting their near-round shape. Aspect ratio is obtained from the major and minor semi-axes of a fitted ellipse, allowing orientation-independent shape analysis. An aspect-ratio threshold above 5 is explicitly used for cracks, not pores. Lack-of-fusion defects are assigned to remaining irregular defects after the other categories are identified. Unmelted particles are recognized through object hierarchy as inclusions located inside a defect. The excerpt does not provide a separate keyhole-pore class or a keyhole-specific circularity, aspect-ratio, or size threshold. Defect size is represented by the circle-equivalent diameter, calculated from area, and used for pore-size distributions, including number- and area-weighted distributions. Although predefined diameter classes are mentioned, their actual thresholds are not included in the supplied excerpt. Thus, the provided framework supports gas-pore and irregular lack-of-fusion discrimination through shape descriptors, but it does not establish the requested keyhole-pore criteria or explicit pore-size cutoffs.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides the geometric descriptors used to classify LPBF pores, but it does not state explicit numerical cutoffs separating lack-of-fusion, keyhole, and gas pores. Pores were characterized by volume, surface area, equivalent size, circularity, aspect ratio, and 3D sphericity. Sphericity equals 1 for a perfect sphere and decreases as the pore becomes irregular or elongated; therefore, gas-inclusion pores are associated with relatively high sphericity and circularity, while elongated keyhole pores have lower values and larger volumes. Circularity is calculated from the pore’s cross-sectional area and perimeter, with 1 indicating a circular section. Aspect ratio is the minimum orthogonal diagonal divided by the maximum; values near 1 indicate equiaxed pores, whereas lower values indicate elongation. The text specifically describes keyhole pores as elongated and having significant volume, and gas pores as spherical and smaller. It does not define a lack-of-fusion criterion in the supplied pages, nor does it provide numerical size thresholds for the three pore classes. The only size-processing thresholds reported are removal of pores smaller than 5 voxels and a smallest detectable equivalent pore diameter of 4.5 µm. Thus, classification in this excerpt is qualitative and descriptor-based rather than governed by stated class boundaries.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides morphology-based criteria for distinguishing LPBF pore regimes, but it does not give an explicit circularity metric or universal size thresholds. Aspect ratio is the primary shape descriptor: values below 0.5 indicate flat, irregular pores, while values above 0.5 indicate spherical pores. Lack-of-fusion pores are therefore characterized as relatively large, irregular, flat-shaped defects, often containing trapped unmelted powder; the reported example had a mean Feret diameter of 0.26 mm and aspect ratio of 0.33, with 45.6% porosity. Gas or metallurgical pores in the intermediate energy-density regime are relatively small and spherical, with a reported mean Feret diameter of 0.05 mm and aspect ratio of 0.65. Keyhole pores form at higher energy density and are described as roundish and slightly larger than gas/metallurgical pores; the reported mean Feret diameter was 0.09 mm and aspect ratio 0.57. Thus, the excerpt supports classification using relative size, Feret diameter, aspect ratio, and qualitative shape descriptors: large/irregular/low-aspect-ratio pores suggest lack of fusion; small/spherical/high-aspect-ratio pores suggest gas or metallurgical porosity; and somewhat larger roundish pores at excessive energy density suggest keyhole porosity. Circularity thresholds are not reported in this passage.

Lack-of-fusion pores are identified as non-spherical and generally irregular, whereas gas pores are described as complete spheres and keyhole pores as semispherical shapes produced by the union of partial spheres. contexts.context: The excerpt concerns duplex/superaustenitic steels rather than LPBF 316L, so its preparation guidance is only indirectly applicable. It warns that prolonged etching causes selective attack and over-polishing produces relief at phase boundaries, distorting measurements. Residual SiO₂ can continue etching and create false contrast; residual Al₂O₃ may embed and alter contrast. Thorough cleaning is essential: remove oil/cutting debris, use ultrasonic cleaning where appropriate, rinse with deionized water, finish with ethanol, and dry without wiping. Electropolishing may improve surfaces but can selectively attack multiphase alloys; vibratory polishing may be preferable when inclusions make electropolishing unsatisfactory.
contexts.question:
What is the best practice for preparing and imaging cross-sections of LPBF 316L thin walls to measure porosity and last-layer melt-pool depth in an SEM, and which artefacts bias the results? Context: laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M, L-PBF) of commercial gas-atomized 316L stainless steel powder (about 15-45 um) on a Concept Laser M2 cusing (CL WRX Control 2.4; two 400 W class continuous-wave Yb fibre lasers at about 1070 nm, only one used; galvanometer scanner; nitrogen or argon; no plate heating; layer thickness 30 or 50 um, not yet confirmed). The machine's production 316L parameter set uses, for the core hatch, 370 W, 1350 mm/s, 0.09 mm hatch spacing and a 130 um spot (P/v = 0.274 J/mm), contours at 100-120 W and 130-220 mm/s with a 50-70 um spot, and an upskin at 200 W, 980 mm/s, 0.075 mm hatch. The build: 12 'comb' parts, each a 44.5 x 12.7 mm base (printed with the production set) carrying 7 thin walls (fins) 1.27 mm thick, 12.7 mm long and 7.6 mm tall on a 7.2 mm pitch. Every wall has its own core and upskin laser power P and scan speed v (contours unchanged): 60 settings from a scrambled Sobol sequence over P = 150-370 W and P/v = 0.09-0.55 J/mm (v about 335-2930 mm/s; about 33-204 J/mm^3 at 30 um layers), plus the production hatch as a control. Three parts stand on each of four removable 88 mm square 316L panels; the fourth panel is turned 90 degrees so its walls run across the recoater instead of along it, and repeats 18 settings and the control, giving 21 pairs printed in both orientations. After the build each part is cut lengthwise near its centreline and between walls 4 and 5, hot-mounted in 1.25 in conductive mounts, ground to the centreline (a section through every wall's thickness and height at mid-length), polished, imaged unetched in an SEM (Thermo Fisher Apreo C) for porosity in each wall's core (at least 0.2 mm from the faces, 1 mm from the base and the top), then etched to reveal the last layer's melt-pool boundaries. The results will be compared with the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module (CALPHAD-based properties; steady-state and transient melt-pool calculations; printability maps of lack of fusion, keyholing and balling), to calibrate and test it, and later builds will choose settings by batch Bayesian optimization.

Answer with citations and DOIs. Quote numbers with the conditions they apply to (material, P, v, spot size and how it was defined, hatch spacing, layer thickness, machine, gas). Prefer primary sources, say where sources disagree, and flag which statements are strongly versus weakly supported. Where a paper gives a data table or an open dataset we could compare against, say exactly where (table or figure number, repository and identifier).

In particular:
1. Cutting (abrasive cut-off versus precision diamond saws; kerf; heat damage), conductive hot mounting and edge retention at the top of a wall, and the grinding and polishing sequence for 316L (SiC grits, diamond, colloidal silica or alumina, times and loads), including how much material to remove to reach a plane and how to stop at it.
2. How polishing changes measured porosity in 316L: smearing that closes pores, pull-out, rounding of pore edges, and how to check (repeat polish, comparison with X-ray CT or Archimedes).
3. Imaging porosity: optical versus SEM BSE versus SE; magnification and pixel size; the smallest pore that should be counted; stitched mosaics; how large an area is needed for a given uncertainty at 0.1%, 1% and 5% porosity (ASTM E1245, E2109, ISO/ASTM 52900 family), and how many sections per specimen.
4. Segmentation and classification: thresholding methods; classifying lack-of-fusion, keyhole and gas pores by size, circularity and aspect ratio, with the thresholds used.
5. Etching 316L to reveal melt-pool boundaries and the cellular structure for SEM and optical imaging (electrolytic oxalic acid, aqua regia, Kalling's no. 2, glyceregia, V2A-Beize, Carpenter's): recipes, times, which works best for melt-pool boundaries, and why porosity must be imaged before etching.
6. Measuring the last layer's melt-pool depth and width in a section through a wall: which pools count, how the section angle to the scan direction distorts them, and how many pools to average.
7. Realistic hands-on time per mount and per SEM image for a set of about 24 mounts.

contexts.context: The excerpt recommends reproducible automated preparation, noting load control improves consistency. A manual sequence uses water-lubricated SiC P240–P600 at 70 rpm, inspecting every 30 s, followed by diamond polishing (6, 3, 1 µm) at 170 rpm. Final SiO₂ removes deformation and scratches; 1 µm may be omitted. OP-S removes scratches more efficiently, whereas OP-U is less aggressive and preserves planarity. No DOI or 316L-specific evidence is provided.

contexts.context: The excerpt is a duplex-stainless-steel preparation guide, not a 316L-specific study. It recommends water-cooled/lubricated precision saws with thin blades and low loads to minimize overheating and deformation; abrasive cut-off blades should be alloy-specific. Thermal cutting (plasma, laser, EDM) can alter microstructure. Deburring is essential. Mounting in phenolic resin or epoxy improves stability; epoxy offers low shrinkage and adhesion but cures for hours and is softer. Tight adhesion minimizes crevices and preserves edges. It emphasizes complete, reproducible preparation over shortcuts, referring readers to ASTM E3 and Vander Voort for detailed procedures.
contexts.question:
What is the best practice for preparing and imaging cross-sections of LPBF 316L thin walls to measure porosity and last-layer melt-pool depth in an SEM, and which artefacts bias the results? Context: laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M, L-PBF) of commercial gas-atomized 316L stainless steel powder (about 15-45 um) on a Concept Laser M2 cusing (CL WRX Control 2.4; two 400 W class continuous-wave Yb fibre lasers at about 1070 nm, only one used; galvanometer scanner; nitrogen or argon; no plate heating; layer thickness 30 or 50 um, not yet confirmed). The machine's production 316L parameter set uses, for the core hatch, 370 W, 1350 mm/s, 0.09 mm hatch spacing and a 130 um spot (P/v = 0.274 J/mm), contours at 100-120 W and 130-220 mm/s with a 50-70 um spot, and an upskin at 200 W, 980 mm/s, 0.075 mm hatch. The build: 12 'comb' parts, each a 44.5 x 12.7 mm base (printed with the production set) carrying 7 thin walls (fins) 1.27 mm thick, 12.7 mm long and 7.6 mm tall on a 7.2 mm pitch. Every wall has its own core and upskin laser power P and scan speed v (contours unchanged): 60 settings from a scrambled Sobol sequence over P = 150-370 W and P/v = 0.09-0.55 J/mm (v about 335-2930 mm/s; about 33-204 J/mm^3 at 30 um layers), plus the production hatch as a control. Three parts stand on each of four removable 88 mm square 316L panels; the fourth panel is turned 90 degrees so its walls run across the recoater instead of along it, and repeats 18 settings and the control, giving 21 pairs printed in both orientations. After the build each part is cut lengthwise near its centreline and between walls 4 and 5, hot-mounted in 1.25 in conductive mounts, ground to the centreline (a section through every wall's thickness and height at mid-length), polished, imaged unetched in an SEM (Thermo Fisher Apreo C) for porosity in each wall's core (at least 0.2 mm from the faces, 1 mm from the base and the top), then etched to reveal the last layer's melt-pool boundaries. The results will be compared with the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module (CALPHAD-based properties; steady-state and transient melt-pool calculations; printability maps of lack of fusion, keyholing and balling), to calibrate and test it, and later builds will choose settings by batch Bayesian optimization.

Answer with citations and DOIs. Quote numbers with the conditions they apply to (material, P, v, spot size and how it was defined, hatch spacing, layer thickness, machine, gas). Prefer primary sources, say where sources disagree, and flag which statements are strongly versus weakly supported. Where a paper gives a data table or an open dataset we could compare against, say exactly where (table or figure number, repository and identifier).

In particular:
1. Cutting (abrasive cut-off versus precision diamond saws; kerf; heat damage), conductive hot mounting and edge retention at the top of a wall, and the grinding and polishing sequence for 316L (SiC grits, diamond, colloidal silica or alumina, times and loads), including how much material to remove to reach a plane and how to stop at it.
2. How polishing changes measured porosity in 316L: smearing that closes pores, pull-out, rounding of pore edges, and how to check (repeat polish, comparison with X-ray CT or Archimedes).
3. Imaging porosity: optical versus SEM BSE versus SE; magnification and pixel size; the smallest pore that should be counted; stitched mosaics; how large an area is needed for a given uncertainty at 0.1%, 1% and 5% porosity (ASTM E1245, E2109, ISO/ASTM 52900 family), and how many sections per specimen.
4. Segmentation and classification: thresholding methods; classifying lack-of-fusion, keyhole and gas pores by size, circularity and aspect ratio, with the thresholds used.
5. Etching 316L to reveal melt-pool boundaries and the cellular structure for SEM and optical imaging (electrolytic oxalic acid, aqua regia, Kalling's no. 2, glyceregia, V2A-Beize, Carpenter's): recipes, times, which works best for melt-pool boundaries, and why porosity must be imaged before etching.
6. Measuring the last layer's melt-pool depth and width in a section through a wall: which pools count, how the section angle to the scan direction distorts them, and how many pools to average.
7. Realistic hands-on time per mount and per SEM image for a set of about 24 mounts.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the measurable quantities from etched LPBF cross-sections as melt-pool welding depth (dmp) and width (wmp), obtained after segmentation of the melt-pool boundaries. It emphasizes that conventional studies generally measure melt pools manually and often restrict the analysis to single tracks or the top layer, because neighboring tracks and subsequent layers remelt earlier pools. The proposed method instead evaluates melt pools throughout the specimen cross-section, including partly visible remelted pools, thereby enabling many pools to be measured and improving statistical analysis. However, these pages do not specify how many melt pools should be averaged, nor do they provide a numerical counting rule for pools in the last layer. Section orientation is important: when the scan direction is rotated by an angle such as 67° between layers, an inclined section plane makes melt pools appear distorted and creates patterns that are more difficult to analyze. The study therefore uses a 90° scan-direction rotation for its melt-pool measurements. The excerpt does not quantify the resulting dimensional error or give a correction formula for section-angle distortion.
contexts.question: How to measure melt pool depth and width from etched cross-sections in LPBF: how many melt pools to average, which pools to count in the last layer, and how the section angle relative to scan direction distorts the apparent melt pool dimensions?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes measuring melt-pool width and depth on etched/metallographic cross-sections using a Keyence VHX-7000 optical microscope and its image-analysis software, at 500× and 1000× magnification. For each single track, width and depth were measured from transverse cross-sectional views and averaged over eight measurements. The top view was instead used to characterize the full track and correlate in-process thermal observations with post-process metallography. Reported uncertainty was approximately ±5–40 μm, combining track-to-track variability with the operator-dependent identification of melt-pool boundaries. The excerpt does not specify how many distinct melt pools should be counted in the final layer, nor does it give a protocol for selecting pools in that layer. It also does not discuss the effect of cutting or sectioning angle relative to the laser scan direction, such as apparent elongation or distortion of melt-pool width and depth. Therefore, the only directly supported averaging instruction is eight cross-sectional measurements per single track; procedures for last-layer pool selection and angular correction must be obtained from another source or methodological context.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides only limited information relevant to measuring melt-pool dimensions from etched LPBF cross-sections. It indicates that vertical metallographic cross-sections of etched 316L stainless-steel parts are used to show melt-pool dimensions and distinguish processing conditions. However, the supplied pages do not state how many melt pools should be measured and averaged, which specific pools should be counted in the final (last) layer, or how the cross-section angle relative to the scan direction changes the apparent depth and width. The text mainly describes an online imaging method for width: a Sobel edge detector identifies the melt-pool outline, and a ruler-line perpendicular to the scan direction passes through the beam center; the distance between its intersections with the outline gives the maximum melt-pool width. For modeling, melt-pool depth is represented by the parameter e and width by d, with their ratio used in an analytical model. The excerpt cautions that actual LPBF pools commonly have a parabola-like cross-section and widths larger than the beam diameter. Therefore, it cannot support a definitive protocol for averaging pools, selecting last-layer pools, or correcting section-angle distortion; those details must come from another section or source.
contexts.question: How to measure melt pool depth and width from etched cross-sections in LPBF: how many melt pools to average, which pools to count in the last layer, and how the section angle relative to scan direction distorts the apparent melt pool dimensions?

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns X-ray computed tomography of LPBF maraging steel rather than image-based porosity measurement in LPBF 316L. It reports a CT voxel size of 1.5 µm, removal of pores smaller than five voxels, and a smallest detectable equivalent pore diameter of 4.5 µm. The authors note that the approximately 1.5 µm resolution introduces a significant error when measuring very small pore volumes, although the error decreases as pore volume increases. The passage does not specify optical magnification, pixel size for metallographic image analysis, the imaging area required to estimate porosity at 0.1%, 1%, or 5%, or recommendations concerning the number of fields. It also does not discuss ASTM E1245 or ASTM E2109. Therefore, these CT resolution values may provide only a rough, technique-specific reference and should not be treated as validated settings or sampling requirements for LPBF 316L optical porosity measurements.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general cautions relevant to selecting image-analysis parameters for LPBF porosity measurement, but it does not give specific recommendations for 316L regarding optical magnification, pixel size, minimum detectable pore size, or imaged area at porosity levels of 0.1%, 1%, and 5%. It emphasizes that microscopic porosity measurements lack a standardized imaging method and can be biased by choices such as magnification, focus, field location, and the number of images analyzed. It also notes that automatic image analysis is being developed to reduce operator-dependent variability. For volumetric methods such as micro-CT, the excerpt explains that resolution must be balanced against scanned volume: higher resolution detects smaller pores but covers less material, while lower resolution permits larger volumes but misses smaller defects. A representative volume should therefore be chosen based on the defect population and the failure mechanism being studied. The excerpt does not state what ASTM E1245 or ASTM E2109 require concerning the number of fields, nor does it provide field-count guidance for the specified porosity levels. Those standards and application-specific validation data would need to be consulted separately.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an LPBF image-analysis procedure using a Zeiss AxioImager at 10× magnification with a pixel size of 0.56 µm, acquired in stitching mode over whole 5 mm-diameter samples. Sections were imaged at multiple depths to enlarge the dataset: 1 mm below the original top surface, followed by additional sections 0.5 mm and 1 mm deeper. Porosity was calculated as the summed area of all detected defects divided by the total analyzed sample area, and defect areas were converted to circle-equivalent diameters for pore-size distributions. However, this passage does not establish a minimum detectable or reportable pore size, and it concerns ferritic X2CrNi12 (AISI 410L), not LPBF 316L. ASTM E1245 and ASTM E2109 are not discussed in the excerpt, so their prescribed or recommended number of fields cannot be determined from this source. The stated 10×/0.56 µm setup and multi-section imaging may be useful as an example, but should not be treated as a validated specification for 316L or for the requested porosity-confidence levels.

contexts.context: Rønneberg, Davies and Hooper (Materials & Design 189, 108481, 2020, DOI: **10.1016/j.matdes.2019.108481**) sectioned LPBF 316L, epoxy-mounted, ground with SiC, polished using diamond to **1 μm**, then **0.06 μm colloidal silica**. Electrolytic etching used **10% oxalic acid, 5 V, 90 s**; SEM imaging at **13 kV, ~8 mm working distance** gave good BSE contrast. Large stitched optical images (**2.61 μm/pixel**, ≥**1000 mm²/section**) were analysed in ImageJ; objects **<25 μm² (<4 pixels)** were excluded as preparation artefacts. Both optical and SEM examination were used.
contexts.question:
What is the best practice for preparing and imaging cross-sections of LPBF 316L thin walls to measure porosity and last-layer melt-pool depth in an SEM, and which artefacts bias the results? Context: laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M, L-PBF) of commercial gas-atomized 316L stainless steel powder (about 15-45 um) on a Concept Laser M2 cusing (CL WRX Control 2.4; two 400 W class continuous-wave Yb fibre lasers at about 1070 nm, only one used; galvanometer scanner; nitrogen or argon; no plate heating; layer thickness 30 or 50 um, not yet confirmed). The machine's production 316L parameter set uses, for the core hatch, 370 W, 1350 mm/s, 0.09 mm hatch spacing and a 130 um spot (P/v = 0.274 J/mm), contours at 100-120 W and 130-220 mm/s with a 50-70 um spot, and an upskin at 200 W, 980 mm/s, 0.075 mm hatch. The build: 12 'comb' parts, each a 44.5 x 12.7 mm base (printed with the production set) carrying 7 thin walls (fins) 1.27 mm thick, 12.7 mm long and 7.6 mm tall on a 7.2 mm pitch. Every wall has its own core and upskin laser power P and scan speed v (contours unchanged): 60 settings from a scrambled Sobol sequence over P = 150-370 W and P/v = 0.09-0.55 J/mm (v about 335-2930 mm/s; about 33-204 J/mm^3 at 30 um layers), plus the production hatch as a control. Three parts stand on each of four removable 88 mm square 316L panels; the fourth panel is turned 90 degrees so its walls run across the recoater instead of along it, and repeats 18 settings and the control, giving 21 pairs printed in both orientations. After the build each part is cut lengthwise near its centreline and between walls 4 and 5, hot-mounted in 1.25 in conductive mounts, ground to the centreline (a section through every wall's thickness and height at mid-length), polished, imaged unetched in an SEM (Thermo Fisher Apreo C) for porosity in each wall's core (at least 0.2 mm from the faces, 1 mm from the base and the top), then etched to reveal the last layer's melt-pool boundaries. The results will be compared with the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module (CALPHAD-based properties; steady-state and transient melt-pool calculations; printability maps of lack of fusion, keyholing and balling), to calibrate and test it, and later builds will choose settings by batch Bayesian optimization.

Answer with citations and DOIs. Quote numbers with the conditions they apply to (material, P, v, spot size and how it was defined, hatch spacing, layer thickness, machine, gas). Prefer primary sources, say where sources disagree, and flag which statements are strongly versus weakly supported. Where a paper gives a data table or an open dataset we could compare against, say exactly where (table or figure number, repository and identifier).

In particular:
1. Cutting (abrasive cut-off versus precision diamond saws; kerf; heat damage), conductive hot mounting and edge retention at the top of a wall, and the grinding and polishing sequence for 316L (SiC grits, diamond, colloidal silica or alumina, times and loads), including how much material to remove to reach a plane and how to stop at it.
2. How polishing changes measured porosity in 316L: smearing that closes pores, pull-out, rounding of pore edges, and how to check (repeat polish, comparison with X-ray CT or Archimedes).
3. Imaging porosity: optical versus SEM BSE versus SE; magnification and pixel size; the smallest pore that should be counted; stitched mosaics; how large an area is needed for a given uncertainty at 0.1%, 1% and 5% porosity (ASTM E1245, E2109, ISO/ASTM 52900 family), and how many sections per specimen.
4. Segmentation and classification: thresholding methods; classifying lack-of-fusion, keyhole and gas pores by size, circularity and aspect ratio, with the thresholds used.
5. Etching 316L to reveal melt-pool boundaries and the cellular structure for SEM and optical imaging (electrolytic oxalic acid, aqua regia, Kalling's no. 2, glyceregia, V2A-Beize, Carpenter's): recipes, times, which works best for melt-pool boundaries, and why porosity must be imaged before etching.
6. Measuring the last layer's melt-pool depth and width in a section through a wall: which pools count, how the section angle to the scan direction distorts them, and how many pools to average.
7. Realistic hands-on time per mount and per SEM image for a set of about 24 mounts.

contexts.context: Rønneberg, Davies and Hooper (Materials & Design 189, 108481, 2020, DOI: **10.1016/j.matdes.2019.108481**) analysed polished LPBF 316L sections with ImageJ “Analyse Particles.” Objects **<25 μm² (<4 pixels)** were excluded as preparation artefacts; pore area, fitted ellipse and Feret diameter were recorded. Large pores were irregular and sometimes particle-containing, consistent with lack of fusion. Because porosity was dominated by a few large pores, large areas (**1099–1232 mm²**) were required: measured area fractions were **0.26–0.66%**, with no pores >400 μm. Size alone could not distinguish keyhole from lack-of-fusion pores; aspect-ratio measurements below **30 μm** were resolution-affected.

contexts.context: The excerpt reviews LPBF 316L residual-stress research, not cross-section preparation or SEM porosity measurement. It reports that thicker layers generally reduce stress/distortion (e.g., 90 vs 30, 60 vs 30, 75 vs 25, and 45 vs 30 µm), attributed to lower cooling rates and thermal gradients; thicker layers also produce deeper melt pools but may reduce density and slightly weaken properties. Larger spots produce wider, flatter pools, yet their stress effect is unclear; one AISI 420 study found increased porosity and reduced density/hardness. The experiment uses Aconity MIDI+, nitrogen, 15–45 µm 316L powder, 1070 nm laser, and 10–500 µm adjustable spots. No DOI is supplied.

contexts.context: Lane et al. describe in-situ melt-pool thermography, not metallographic preparation of LPBF 316L cross-sections. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that chemical etching can substantially modify the apparent morphology surrounding LPBF pores and defects, making pre-etch imaging important for reliable porosity characterization. In low-energy material, pores and lack-of-fusion defects are associated with unfused powder, incomplete molten-metal filling, and non-filled gaps. At the optimal energy density, defects were small and spherical, whereas excessive energy input caused over-melting, very large grains, reduced corrosion resistance, and corrosion trenches in the melt pools. These trenches and grooves are produced by the corrosion/etching process rather than necessarily representing original pores, and they can obscure, enlarge, split, or visually resemble pore boundaries. Consequently, porosity measurements made only after etching may confuse etch-induced grooves or preferentially corroded regions with true voids and may alter estimates of pore size, shape, number, and area fraction. The excerpt also contrasts conditions where pores were clearly visible with etched microstructures in which pores were “almost invisible,” showing that etching can affect defect visibility in either direction. Imaging the unetched surface first preserves the original pore geometry; etched metallography can then be used separately to study melt-pool structure, lack of fusion, and microstructural development.
contexts.question: Why must porosity be imaged before etching in metallographic analysis of LPBF parts? How does etching affect pore boundaries and porosity measurements?

It does, however, describe the limitations of destructive metallographic approaches such as optical microscopy and SEM: they analyze only selected cross-sectional regions, and the polished area may not represent the entire LPBF specimen. A section that appears free of defects can conceal defects beneath the surface, so measurements based on one section may not capture the full porosity distribution. The table characterizes optical and SEM methods as destructive and capable of detailed defect characterization, but their results remain dependent on the examined cross-section. These points provide general context for interpreting metallographic porosity measurements, while the specific rationale for imaging before etching and the effects of etching on pore-boundary definition are not covered in the supplied pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not directly discuss etching or require imaging before etching. It does show why the initial, unetched metallographic image is important for reliable comparison: optical microscopy (OM) provides a 2D measurement of pore area and shape, whereas X-ray CT provides 3D pore volume and morphology. A 2D section can make a pore appear more circular depending on the plane intersected, and therefore may overestimate circularity or aspect ratio and fail to represent the pore’s non-uniform three-dimensional boundary. The authors report that 3D analysis gives a broader and more accurate distribution of pore dimensions, while 2D measurements can produce different apparent morphology and porosity values. Consequently, any preparation step that changes contrast or the apparent pore boundary—including etching—could alter segmentation, measured pore area, circularity, and calculated porosity. Imaging before etching preserves the original polished-section boundary and provides a baseline; post-etch images should be interpreted cautiously because etching may reveal, obscure, or visually modify pore edges and nearby material. The excerpt supports the general measurement concern but does not specify the direction or magnitude of etching-induced changes.
contexts.question: Why must porosity be imaged before etching in metallographic analysis of LPBF parts? How does etching affect pore boundaries and porosity measurements?

contexts.context: The excerpt does not directly discuss metallographic etching or specify how etching changes pore boundaries. It does establish why an unetched image is important as a baseline: optical microscopy is a destructive, two-dimensional method that can be affected by selection bias, and pore morphology is used to distinguish pore types. Gas pores are generally small and spherical, whereas lack-of-fusion pores are larger and irregular. Consequently, imaging before etching preserves the original exposed pore geometry and allows pore size, shape, and area fraction to be assessed before any preparation step potentially modifies or obscures the boundaries. The excerpt also cautions that porosity measurements depend strongly on the characterization method. Optical microscopy provides detailed information but only in 2D; computed tomography is nondestructive and three-dimensional, although resolution, analyzed volume, cost, and filtering can affect accuracy and may lead to porosity underestimation. Thus, the source supports the need for a consistent pre-etch reference and awareness of measurement bias, but it does not provide direct evidence about the specific effects of etching on pore walls or measured porosity.
contexts.question: Why must porosity be imaged before etching in metallographic analysis of LPBF parts? How does etching affect pore boundaries and porosity measurements?

contexts.context: The excerpt supports imaging LPBF porosity by X-ray CT before metallographic preparation because CT records the three-dimensional internal pore network without sectioning or surface preparation. It can identify both elongated keyhole pores and spherical gas-inclusion pores, measure their volumes and surface areas, and calculate three-dimensional shape descriptors such as sphericity and aspect ratio. Metallographic optical microscopy, by contrast, examines only selected polished cross-sections and determines pore size from two-dimensional pixel measurements; therefore, it can miss pores between sections or distort their apparent geometry. The excerpt does not specifically report an etching experiment or quantify how etching changes pore boundaries. It does establish that pore measurements depend on image segmentation, resolution, polishing, and the measurement method. Consequently, any etching that changes, obscures, or visually redefines the material–void interface could alter the apparent pore perimeter and area in optical images, affecting circularity, aspect ratio, and estimated porosity. CT data acquired before etching provide a reference for the original pore morphology and volume. The study also cautions that limited resolution produces greater error for very small pore volumes, while the error decreases as pore volume increases.

contexts.context: NIST AMS 100-3 states that porosity, voids, cracks, and delaminations in AM materials may be evaluated destructively by cutting, cleaning, mounting, grinding, and polishing, following ASTM E3 and ISO 4505; ISO 4499-4 and ISO 4505 provide reference porosity photomicrographs. Nondestructive methods are also discussed, with ASTM E543 listing detectable flaws and method advantages. ASTM E1245 supports automated reflected-light microscopy or SEM image analysis using grey-level detection to measure feature counts, areas, and spacing, but small fields may require extensive sampling. contexts.question:
What is the best practice for preparing and imaging cross-sections of LPBF 316L thin walls to measure porosity and last-layer melt-pool depth in an SEM, and which artefacts bias the results? Context: laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M, L-PBF) of commercial gas-atomized 316L stainless steel powder (about 15-45 um) on a Concept Laser M2 cusing (CL WRX Control 2.4; two 400 W class continuous-wave Yb fibre lasers at about 1070 nm, only one used; galvanometer scanner; nitrogen or argon; no plate heating; layer thickness 30 or 50 um, not yet confirmed). The machine's production 316L parameter set uses, for the core hatch, 370 W, 1350 mm/s, 0.09 mm hatch spacing and a 130 um spot (P/v = 0.274 J/mm), contours at 100-120 W and 130-220 mm/s with a 50-70 um spot, and an upskin at 200 W, 980 mm/s, 0.075 mm hatch. The build: 12 'comb' parts, each a 44.5 x 12.7 mm base (printed with the production set) carrying 7 thin walls (fins) 1.27 mm thick, 12.7 mm long and 7.6 mm tall on a 7.2 mm pitch. Every wall has its own core and upskin laser power P and scan speed v (contours unchanged): 60 settings from a scrambled Sobol sequence over P = 150-370 W and P/v = 0.09-0.55 J/mm (v about 335-2930 mm/s; about 33-204 J/mm^3 at 30 um layers), plus the production hatch as a control. Three parts stand on each of four removable 88 mm square 316L panels; the fourth panel is turned 90 degrees so its walls run across the recoater instead of along it, and repeats 18 settings and the control, giving 21 pairs printed in both orientations. After the build each part is cut lengthwise near its centreline and between walls 4 and 5, hot-mounted in 1.25 in conductive mounts, ground to the centreline (a section through every wall's thickness and height at mid-length), polished, imaged unetched in an SEM (Thermo Fisher Apreo C) for porosity in each wall's core (at least 0.2 mm from the faces, 1 mm from the base and the top), then etched to reveal the last layer's melt-pool boundaries. The results will be compared with the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module (CALPHAD-based properties; steady-state and transient melt-pool calculations; printability maps of lack of fusion, keyholing and balling), to calibrate and test it, and later builds will choose settings by batch Bayesian optimization.

Answer with citations and DOIs. Quote numbers with the conditions they apply to (material, P, v, spot size and how it was defined, hatch spacing, layer thickness, machine, gas). Prefer primary sources, say where sources disagree, and flag which statements are strongly versus weakly supported. Where a paper gives a data table or an open dataset we could compare against, say exactly where (table or figure number, repository and identifier).

In particular:
1. Cutting (abrasive cut-off versus precision diamond saws; kerf; heat damage), conductive hot mounting and edge retention at the top of a wall, and the grinding and polishing sequence for 316L (SiC grits, diamond, colloidal silica or alumina, times and loads), including how much material to remove to reach a plane and how to stop at it.
2. How polishing changes measured porosity in 316L: smearing that closes pores, pull-out, rounding of pore edges, and how to check (repeat polish, comparison with X-ray CT or Archimedes).
3. Imaging porosity: optical versus SEM BSE versus SE; magnification and pixel size; the smallest pore that should be counted; stitched mosaics; how large an area is needed for a given uncertainty at 0.1%, 1% and 5% porosity (ASTM E1245, E2109, ISO/ASTM 52900 family), and how many sections per specimen.
4. Segmentation and classification: thresholding methods; classifying lack-of-fusion, keyhole and gas pores by size, circularity and aspect ratio, with the thresholds used.
5. Etching 316L to reveal melt-pool boundaries and the cellular structure for SEM and optical imaging (electrolytic oxalic acid, aqua regia, Kalling's no. 2, glyceregia, V2A-Beize, Carpenter's): recipes, times, which works best for melt-pool boundaries, and why porosity must be imaged before etching.
6. Measuring the last layer's melt-pool depth and width in a section through a wall: which pools count, how the section angle to the scan direction distorts them, and how many pools to average.
7. Realistic hands-on time per mount and per SEM image for a set of about 24 mounts.

contexts.context: NIST’s AM standards review recommends ASTM E3-based metallography: choose location/orientation deliberately, report longitudinal/transverse/build directions, and use sawing, abrasive cut-off, or shearing to minimize structural alteration (NIST AMS 100-3, DOI: **10.6028/NIST.AMS.100-3**). ASTM E407 supplies etchant compositions/procedures; ASTM E1245/E768 address image analysis and specimen quality. LPBF anisotropy requires analyses parallel and perpendicular to build direction (also ASTM F2971, F3122; ISO/ASTM 52921). Existing standards are general, not AM-specific: preparation is often “trial and error,” and representative location, number, and direction of sections are critical.

contexts.context: Bahshwan’s 2026 article presents 2-D image segmentation as a low-cost alternative to CT: optical images are thresholded, segmented, and morphologically analyzed (Figure 1). CT provides quantitative 3-D pore morphology but is expensive; Archimedes gives only volume-averaged density, without pore size, shape, or distribution. The study examines 316L LPBF surface porosity and reports lack-of-fusion reduction from 30 to 70 W (75.8 J/mm³), tenfold smaller surface pores from 30 to 90 W, and RAPID validation against ImageJ. RAPID is open-source on GitHub, but this excerpt supplies no metallographic preparation, SEM, etching, melt-pool, uncertainty, or artefact protocols. DOI: **10.3390/ma19214527**.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents RAPID, a free, open-source MATLAB/ImageJ-like workflow for reproducible LPBF-316L porosity analysis, motivated by poorly documented thresholds, morphology settings, and image counts (Bahshwan et al., *Materials* 2026, 19, 4527, DOI: **10.3390/ma19214527**). Gas-atomized 316L was printed on a Concept Mlab cusing using a 50-µm nominal beam, 30–90 W, 600 mm/s, 77-µm hatch, and 20-µm layers; surfaces were polished to **Ra <800 nm**. Nine 20× bright-field optical images per specimen were acquired, with debris, scratches, and shadows manually removed. RAPID supports cropping, contrast enhancement, vignetting correction, pixel calibration, segmentation, morphology analysis, and export.

The results will be compared with the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module (CALPHAD-based properties; steady-state and transient melt-pool calculations; printability maps of lack of fusion, keyholing and balling), to calibrate and test it, and later builds will choose settings by batch Bayesian optimization.

Answer with citations and DOIs. Quote numbers with the conditions they apply to (material, P, v, spot size and how it was defined, hatch spacing, layer thickness, machine, gas). Prefer primary sources, say where sources disagree, and flag which statements are strongly versus weakly supported. Where a paper gives a data table or an open dataset we could compare against, say exactly where (table or figure number, repository and identifier).

In particular:
1. Cutting (abrasive cut-off versus precision diamond saws; kerf; heat damage), conductive hot mounting and edge retention at the top of a wall, and the grinding and polishing sequence for 316L (SiC grits, diamond, colloidal silica or alumina, times and loads), including how much material to remove to reach a plane and how to stop at it.
2. How polishing changes measured porosity in 316L: smearing that closes pores, pull-out, rounding of pore edges, and how to check (repeat polish, comparison with X-ray CT or Archimedes).
3. Imaging porosity: optical versus SEM BSE versus SE; magnification and pixel size; the smallest pore that should be counted; stitched mosaics; how large an area is needed for a given uncertainty at 0.1%, 1% and 5% porosity (ASTM E1245, E2109, ISO/ASTM 52900 family), and how many sections per specimen.
